Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106, it is my duty to present to the House a petition signed by residents of Canada who, when visiting the Byward market this summer, cared enough to write their name and address on this petition which says that since September, 1984, the federal Government has imposed on Canadian taxpayers 25 new taxes or increases in existing taxes, including some on medical and dental supplies, snack foods, candies, and soft drinks; that in its White Paper on tax reform the federal Government is considering the possibility of imposing on Canadian taxpayers a general tax on goods and services, including foodstuff; that foods represents a vital element in their daily lives and this sales tax would heavily penalize various categories of taxpayers, including senior citizens, families, the unemployed, low and middle income taxpayers, the young, etc.
Wherefore, the undersigned humbly pray and call upon Parliament to turn down any legislation whose effect would be to impose a sales tax on foodstuff.

August 17, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976

The House resumed from Tuesday, August 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard that Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and the amendment of Mr. Marchi, (p. 7338).

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) who had the floor when the Bill was last debated. My question deals with the safe third country clause in the Bill. All Members have received a letter from the English speaking section of Amnesty International which says that the organization is extremely concerned that proposed new refugee legislation could lead to serious errors with genuine refugees.
As we know, the legislation before us could possibly give the authorities power to return persons forcibly to countries where they may expect to be arbitrarily detained for the non-violent expression of their beliefs, or even tortured or executed.
Could the Member give us the benefit of his knowledge and experience in this matter with regard to persons coming to Canada being returned to a safe third country? That concept is a new one in Bill C-55. People in my riding question me about that and 1 wonder whether the Member for Davenport has some comments to make on that concept?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. As you probably know, we all received a letter from Amnesty International signed by the chairperson of the Refugee Coordination Group. Through that letter Amnesty International is bringing to the attention of Members of Parliament the fact that it is extremely concerned that Bill C-55 could lead to serious errors in that genuine refugees could be sent back to their country of origin to face possible persecution.
The letter goes on to indicate that Amnesty International believes that no Canadian would knowingly risk the security of genuine refugees. I know that that sentiment is well placed and reflects very clearly the sentiment of the majority of Canadians on this matter.
In this letter, Amnesty International brought to our attention a letter which they wrote on August 7 to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in which they expressed their views quite well in the first paragraph which I will put on record. It begins by saying that Amnesty International is writing to the Prime Minister-
-in response to the recent introduction of Bill C-55 which, if passed into
law, will dramatically change Canada's refugee determination policy. As you
may be aware. Amnesty International opposes the forcible return of persons to
countries where they may reasonably be expected to be arbitrarily detained for the non-violent expression of their beliefs, tortured or executed.
A law which increases the likelihood of such events occurring is therefore of great concern to our organization.
I am sure that Amnesty International is speaking on behalf of many Canadians. That letter, signed by Robert Goodfellow, president of Amnesty International, concludes as follows:
We urge you and your government to amend or withdraw and replace Bill C-55 with legislation which incorporates the fundamental principles of universal access, an appeal on the merits and independent decision-making.
We would be very wise and well served to pay very close attention to that letter from Amnesty International.

Mr. Speaker, I am especially interested in the comments of Amnesty International that the Bill should be amended. I want to bring to the attention of the Hon. Member that we are presently discussing an amendment moved by his colleague, the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), to delay discussion of this Bill until some time in 1988. Amendments can be made at committee stage as suggested by Amnesty International and the Bill can be improved. However, his colleague's amendment would delay discussion of the refugee determination Bill until 1988.
I have two questions for my hon. colleague. First, will he be voting with his colleague from York West to further delay discussion of the refugee determination system until some time next year?
The second question is the most important. In the Hon. Member's riding of Davenport there are a great many new Canadians who came to this country and met the requirements and regulations for medical and security clearance and did not jump the queue. How will his law-abiding constituents, new Canadians, feel about him voting in favour of a further six-month delay of this Bill with no discussion at committee stage?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Parliamentary Secretary for his questions because they are relevant. First, I am glad to hear that he is amenable to and attracted by the motion of amendments. That is good news because if amendments were to be initiated by him or any other member of the Progressive Conservative Party who can speak with authority on this Bill indicating that the questions of access and universality are resolved, we would be very glad to take a positive look at this Bill because it would coincide exactly with the concerns raised by Amnesty International.
However, we have not yet heard anything about that. So far the signals from the Government have been to the contrary. As the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) indicated in debate last week, we had to move a motion to hoist the Bill out of sheer desperation when it became clear that the Government was not listening.
Most Canadians do not know that this Bill was only introduced for first reading in this House on May 5. After two and one-half years in which to mull it over, with a phenomenal
August 17, 1987

amount of input from Mr. Plaut, Mr. Ratushney and Mr. Robinson, the Bill sat waiting for debate from May 5 to June 18. It then had a three-hour debate and, to our astonishment, was put aside by the Government.
I do not know what game the Government is playing on this matter. If it had serious intentions on this Bill and wanted to have it passed, it would have indicated its willingness to change it at second reading along the lines suggested by many, not only in the Opposition, but in the vast community which is understandably interested in this matter. We would have made progress. For the life of me, I cannot understand why we are facing such a stonewall.

Mr. Speaker, in the riding I represent, in the Montreal area, 30 per cent of my constituents are either immigrants or descendants of immigrants. They are watching the proceedings with a great deal of interest, and they were watching last week as well. I had a chance to meet some of them personally, and I received about 150 phone calls from people who were in favour of new immigration legislation that would make some changes in the way immigrants are treated here, the way they can enter the country and especially the way refugees or phony refugees come to settle in Canada.
On the week-end 1 met with people from the Maritimes, especially in the Magdalen Islands. Madam Speaker, not many immigrants go to the Magdalen Islands. In fact, the people who live there try to get away. We go there because we think it is a very scenic and interesting place. Over there, they watch the proceedings in the House and wonder what all the fuss is about. They watch what is going on, Madam Speaker, and they tell us there is a bunch of Opposition Members who want to delay the passage of badly needed legislation.
Madam Speaker, we have all kinds of ways to discuss this Bill, to amend it and improve it if necessary, but the motion before the House today, which we are debating now, says to take the Bill back and table it again in six months. Madam Speaker, I do not know whether you realize when that is going to be, in six months but it will certainly be the spring of 1988, which means practically a year, if we consider the periods when the House is sitting and when it is not. Meanwhile, people who came to Canada previously and who have already become Canadian citizens cannot ask family members- fathers, mothers, brothers or sisters-to come and settle here legally because it takes so long under the present legislation. Madam Speaker, last year in my riding, I saw a gentleman who wanted to bring his sister-in-law to Canada to attend her sister's wedding. He applied for a one-month tourist visa. Do you know when he got his tourist visa. Madam Speaker? Six months after the wedding. And that happens all the time. We have no way of speeding up this procedure which means that in no time flat, we have all kinds of refugees coming into this country more or less legally, and then they want us to postpone the debate.
Immigration Act, 1976
Madam Speaker, I think the motion before the House today should be rejected and the Bill passed and referred to a committee of the House for consideration. The Parliamentary Secretary said earlier, and the Minister said so as well on the week-end, that the Bill could be amended if necessary. Madam Speaker, in the three years we have been sitting in this House, not a single Bill has been sent to committee without there being an opportunity to amend or improve it at that stage. I believe there have even been proposals or motions from the Opposition on amendments that had already been approved in Committee. Let no one say it is impossible to change or improve this Bill. That is just not true, Madam Speaker.
You know, when they cannot think of anything to say about a piece of legislation, they try and find all kinds of ways to make the person who presented the legislation look bad. Last week, Madam Speaker, I was listening carefully to the speeches made by opposition Members, both on the Liberal and the NDP side, and they were doing their best to have Canadians believe that this would be a very dangerous Bill if it were approved as is, because it would mean that organizations working to help refugees, such as the churches and Amnesty International, might be penalized. Madam Speaker, they even said, in fact, it was the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) who said that we should send the Stastny brothers back to their country because of the way they entered this country. Well now, I would suggest that if demagoguery has a home it has to be here in the House of Commons where we can hear such speeches. As if we were going to deport an individual who is already established here after going through the whole determination process. As if we were going to slap a $500,000 fine on church officials doing their best to help refugees. Or as if the Quebec Nordiques management will have to put up $500,000 because they have the Stastny brothers under contract.
Madam Speaker, I would point out to the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides that the Stastny brothers are Canadian citizens and, as such, have nothing to fear. The way he was talking it sounded as though he would send them back. He wanted the Quebec Nordiques to be punished for that. I should think there has to be a limit somewhere.
Madam Speaker, Bill C-55 seeks to set things straight and redress an anomaly caused by refugees who abuse the system and carriers anxious to make a fast buck. You know, a refugee is an individual who fears for his health and whose life may be at stake in his own country, and this individual is only seeking refuge in another country where he will feel safer. Why should he be concerned about his life? I think the answer is very simple: people in some countries are simply not allowed to act democratically the way we do here. They are not free to express their views, they are not free to practise their religion, they are not free to speak their mother tongue. When they do speak out they are frustrated, they feel threatened, so they ask to come here. But of course there are others who are profiteers, others still who are real terrorists or labelled as being undesirable in their own countries. They too fear for their lives, so

August 17, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
they ask us to accept them here. But what are we supposed to do when 175 people land on our shores, how do we decide whether they are real or bogus refugees, particularly when they have no documents, when they have thrown passports, visas and identification papers away? Impossible! We simply have to find a way to determine as quickly as possible whether such individuals are eligible for refugee status here in Canada.
As it happens, Madam Speaker, current legislation provides that certain applicants are eligible, but they have to go through so many stages before they can be accepted or sent back to their own country that in some cases they may have to wait for four or five years before getting an answer. So what do they do in the meantime? We put them up in hotels and, from a social security standpoint, they enjoy most of the rights we Canadians have. They are fed and housed by Canadians, they are expected to wait there without the right to leave, without anything. Meanwhile, the landed immigrants who are already here and who in time have become Canadian citizens cannot use the normal channels to bring over their parents.
In my own riding, there are some 30 per cent of the 115,000 people of Lebanese, Greek, Portuguese, Jewish and Italian descent-altogether some 40,000 people-who feel frustrated and who constantly ask the Government to stop being unfair to them. There are people who come to see me and say: Would it be possible for my old father and mother, who are still in the old country, to come and live their remaining days with us here? They are both 75 years of age. The two of them are alone over there, all their children now live here in Canada or the United States, and we should like them to come and live with us. Considering the time needed to process their application, they would probably die before arriving here. Now, we are being asked to postpone the debate on this Bill. I find this inhuman and abominable.
Although 1 am not very old. Madam Speaker, I have witnessed many things in my life, including people being treated like cattle, and that is almost what is being done now.
By postponing the possibility for these people to come here legally, without endangering either the country and its inhabitants, we are certainly acting in an inhuman fashion.
Madam Speaker, I think that both opposition Parties should be able to accept that and to vote as quickly as possible on second reading of this Bill, and then to refer it to a committee of the House. I agree that the House should accept any constructive amendment which could speed up the process and make life easier. 1 for one would be the first to vote for that, Madam Speaker. For once, however, they should stop playing politics with human beings.
Madam Speaker, the carriers-and I would like to come back to this-take advantage of the situation. You know, Madam Speaker, when there is a loophole in a legislation, given the communication systems we have in North America, it does not take time for the gap to be detected and known
throughout the world. And there will always be some unscrupulous people who will try to exploit it. Such is the case of those accommodating carriers.
Madam Speaker, those carriers take some 150 or 200 individuals in the hold of their ship, allowing them to leave a so-called refugee producing country to bring them to Canada and charge them $1,000 or $2,000 per capita, thus making a profit of $150,000 to $200,000. I doubt very much that those carriers will issue receipts for income tax purposes. 1 also doubt very much that such a carrier will declare that income in his own tax return because I suppose that it is paid in cash.
This is where the abuse is. Those individuals will stop at nothing to make believe to so-called refugees, whether they are legal or not, that they will be admitted. You want to come? I charge $1,000 and you only have to embark. As for the conditions of the trip, that is another ball game. Madam Speaker. They do not care that those people will almost starve to death, become ill during two, three weeks or a month, they will do it for money. We should also take that into account in our legislation, Madam Speaker. We must take steps to put a stop to such abuses. That was the issue debated last week when we dealt with Bill C-84 which will put some teeth in the legislation and impose some punishment or fines to those carriers.
Madam Speaker, I personally view this Bill, actually Bills C-55 and C-84 as very good pieces of legislation. Of course, one cannot be perfect when tabling a Bill or reading it, there are certainly details to be improved upon or changed. But as a matter of principle, I think we have enough backbone to rise and say: Listen, Canada is not a one way street. We open our doors, no problem. You are welcome here, except that you are going to comply with our laws. You will respect the rights of individuals who are already here, and above all you will comply with the procedure for immigrating, for entering our country.
If, when an immigrant comes here, someone suggests: That guy will take my job, 1 do not believe a word of that. Madam Speaker. Legal immigrants come here for different reasons.
It may be family reasons, or economic reasons. Or again, refugees may be involved. But the economic aspect is very important, because when they come here, often they come to create jobs-to start up a company, or to become distributors between European, South American and North American countries. They create jobs, rather than steal them. Nobody here in Canada, Madam Speaker, can come up and say that an immigrant came to this country and took his job. If it happened, it is because of his incompetence. And if it did not happen, a job has been created, because you seldom see a lot of those people depending on welfare. Of the 30 percent of my constituents who are immigrants, Madam Speaker, I can tell you that you can practically count on the fingers of one hand those who are really unemployed in my constituency of Laval.
August 17, 1987

They are motivated people, they come here because it is a new country, a great, vast and rich country, and they know they can do business with its people.
Madam Speaker, we should be fair to our people, to the immigrants who are here and those who want to come, and we also must be fair to the refugees who would settle here.
1 do not know whether opposition Members will support us when the Bill is put to a vote, later today, 1 imagine. I hope that they will because, as I said earlier, Madam Speaker, I met people from the Maritimes during the week-end and they are really fed up with the behavior of the opposition Parties in this debate as they believe that delaying passage of such a Bill will delay the evolution of Canada.
Thank you, Madam Speaker, for giving me this time to express my views, and I hope that we shall be able to put together a good piece of legislation under which everyone will be treated equitably and Canada will be a better country.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy).

Madam Speaker, there are a few comments that I would like to make to the Hon. Member who, on the one hand, is in favour of increased immigration and says on behalf of his constituents that they are frustrated by the problems which arise when they want to have old relatives from overseas come to Canada as immigrants.
I share his concerns in this regard. The present delays are indeed bad, and these delays exist after three years of a Conservative Government. We can wonder why, if the Government is really concerned about this problem, it has done nothing about the delays, not here in Canada, but in immigration offices abroad.
How does the coming to Canada of refugee claimants affect the administrative delays outside Canada? This is my first question.
The second is this: How could Bill C-55 affect the situation of old relatives, for instance, who are now subject to unacceptable delays, since there is no queue, as some have said, since refugees cannot be placed on a waiting list? They either arrive or not.
This does not affect the problem of the delays, which is related to the administration, and to the act and regulations which were developed by the former Liberal Government and accepted for three years by this Conservative Government.
Can the Hon. Member tell us how Bill C-55 can affect the situation and the legitimate concerns of his constituents and why the Conservatives have tried to blame the refugees for their administrative failures when they are due to an administrative problem created by the Government?

Madam Speaker, I should like to respond to the first allegation made by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) to the effect that the legislation has been on the back burner for quite some time. He certainly cannot accuse us of creating this measure. We did not draft it, it was there all along exactly as it is now. It has to be amended and he knows that.
Immigration Act, 1976
Second, Madam Speaker, he is blaming us for a three-year delay in bringing in amendments to the legislation. I wish he would check the motion under consideration right now, and then see for himself who is holding up the debate. We on the Government side? At least we had enough backbone to open up the debate, something which the previous Liberal administration never got around to doing. Since your Party has never been in office, you did not do anything either.
So are you going to support the six-month hoist motion of the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi)? Or are you going to vote on the Government side? In committee, are you going to move constructive amendments or destructive amendments designed to make the Government lose face, whereas you know full well you are the ones who are delaying the debate?
Madam Speaker, I have no idea what the Hon. Member is driving at, but he knows as well that all the publicity surrounding this debate and the refugees who landed on our shores have created a real bottleneck in the various embassies and in the Department of Immigration, with the result that people seeking to go through the normal process come under closer scrutiny than before. Some 18,000 refugees are now waiting for their investigation, waiting to find out whether they will be granted immigrant status or asked to go back home.
Do you know what that means, Madam Speaker? When will these people be allowed in? When will officials working on these cases have time to examine other files? The Department of Immigration has to look after refugee and immigrant cases. Both types of applicants and everything involved. And you want us to delay the whole process? Shame on you!

Mr. Speaker, it is somewhat unfair for my colleague from the government benches to simply concentrate his debate on the suggestion that the Opposition is in a mood to oppose for the sake of opposing. This is very curious when one considers that for three years he has been a member of the the Conservative Government which has had four different Ministers of Immigration. Each of them came into office making a strong statement toward reforming the system.
There have been a number of government-commissioned reports advocating action. There was a unanimous report from the Standing Committee, chaired by a government Member and comprised of a majority of government Members, which suggested a solution to this dilemma, with a system that is out of date having regard to the new phenomenon that developed in the early 1980s. Many NGOs and church organizations have suggested action for nearly three years. The Government has had an absolute majority but has done nothing for three years. I suggest that it is somewhat intellectually dishonest for it to suggest that the reason for the delay is because of the Opposition. I do not believe Canadians are that naive or that gullible.

August 17, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
The Government has a majority and controls the agenda. It could have moved on that reform some time in the last three years rather than the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) waking up on a sunny summer morning suddenly saying that something must be done.
The reason the technical amendment was moved when Bill C-55 came before the House was that there was a mood on the Government side that somehow it would rush this through without thinking of the repercussions. The repercussions, as with Bill C-84, are that unless there is a proper piece of legislation it will be subject to charter and court challenges from one coast to the other. Those challenges will not come from the Opposition but from lawyers and various groups.
I ask the Member to consider what will happen to the legislation. There will be a policy that is more chaotic, more unworkable and more uncertain than the one we have now. It will be difficult to try to get the patience and confidence of Canadians. After three years, Canadians expect the Government to come to grips with the situation in a way that will result in a policy that is not designed for an emergency during the summer or for a couple of months, but that will work well in the long term so that Canadians can give it their support and trust. If we are going to move from this system to one that will be marred by legalities and uncertainties, then we will be testing the patience of Canadians. 1 believe their frustration and anger toward the Government for being either unprepared or unwilling to come to grips with the situation will then turn and transfer itself very dangerously in terms of the global policy.
How does the Government intend to get public support for its desire to have more immigrants come to this country, as it has suggested, when its refugee policy is simply in chaos? Rather than try to blame the opposition Parties, why did it take three years to present new legislation?
If we are going to get a new refugee board, as stipulated in Bill C-55, will he explain why he wants to build a barrier around that with a pre-screening mechanism and a safe third country concept that will make prejudicial statements before there is access to the refugee board?
Everyone agrees with the refugee board. However, under Bill C-55, the Government would be able to dictate or restrict access to the system.
Why is he not prepared to allow refugees full access to the board and allow the board to make a determination, either positively or negatively?

Mr. Speaker, I believe Canadians are testing the Hon. Member who tries to delay the debate. I am very surprised that he has made that suggestion because he was the first to move the motion to delay the Bill we are debating now.
I suggest he will have more than enough time in committee to present some amendments in order to improve the Bill. I believe it is his duty to do so. If he does not, Canadians will judge him.

Madam Speaker, many Canadians have been watching this debate that has been taking place for some time and has reached its peak with Bill C-84 and C-55.
When one considers the atmosphere in which this debate is taking place, there can be no doubt that there is a great deal of concern about abuses to our immigration and refugee determination policies. There has been much criticism and concern expressed about this.
There is concern about legitimate refugees to this country who are really in fear of persecution in their home countries, and that under the processes designed to admit new immigrants into this country there is much delay and difficulty and many refusals for entry of relatives of people who previously immigrated to Canada.
There is much concern that those who are somehow delaying the process are preventing family members of immigrants to get into this country in a reasonable period of time. Some believe that the Department of Employment and Immigration does not act fundamentally to bring more people into this country in order to contribute to the growth of our economy.
It has to be frankly stated that there are those who oppose any kind of immigration, whether it be by refugees or others, on the basis that new immigrants and refugees will take jobs from Canadians. It has been expressed occasionally within and outside the House that those people coming into this country are not the same as Canadians and somehow do not fit into our ways but would be accepted if they acted like the rest of us and adopted the nature of the country to which they are coming.
It is unfortunate, but one often hears in English Canada that those in Quebec do not understand or fit into their ways. We also hear in Quebec similar remarks with respect to English Canadians and those coming from outside. There are a great many attitudes and concerns, some legitimate, some xenophobic, which underlie this whole debate. I think it has to be said, in terms of general consideration of those who come to our country from elsewhere, that there has been a very serious failure on the part of governments, not just this Government but previous Governments, to come to grips with the fact. Yes, we are bringing in people who are different from ourselves, those who are deprived, jobless and fearful of their futures, and there is a notion that immigrants and refugees will take away our jobs. In many cases that may be so, but it is also true that there would exist no Canada whatsoever without immigrants and a very different Canada if there had been no refugees entering our country going back to the 18th century.
August 17, 1987

I have not heard enough about the fact that immigrants and refugees ultimately contribute to our economy. I was impressed by a statistic reported yesterday morning on radio, that there are some 94,000 jobs a year taken away from Canadians by immigrants and refugees. On the other hand, these refugees and immigrants contribute about 115,000 jobs. So there is quite a significant increase of some 20,000 jobs created each year even at the present level of immigration.
Having said that, 1 think it is important to point out that if there existed in Canada a policy for the creation of jobs for Canadians as a specific goal of Government, there would not be the fear that immigrants would take away jobs. People might recognize with greater facility the significant and economic contribution immigrants make by creating jobs.
It seems to me we have not taken a positive approach to this issue, which is an important issue when one considers the most significant motive and perhaps the most reasonable for the free trade negotiations, that is, Canada has too small a marketplace with its 25 million people, and we are not producing enough offspring to maintain our present market size. The reasonable approach to an insufficient population in dealing with a large market is not to become part of the United States but to make Canada larger.
When I considered these facts, I became shocked by the tone of the debate. Politicians are often subject to criticism for their opportunism, for their narrow view of things upon which they act and their tendency to react to critical situations in an opportunistic way. What better situation could have been created than the landing of 174 Sikhs in Nova Scotia following the landing of the Tamils in Newfoundland a year ago? What better circumstance for the great concern, xenophobic and otherwise, which has been evinced by the Canadian people?
There is no doubt the Canadian people see abuses and that they want to see more speed in dealing with these abuses in our system. One might have expected that, instead of waiting until we reached a debate of critical dimensions, the Government might have acted. It seems to me quite evident that if the legislation which was recommended by so many in this country to speed up the refugee determination process had been implemented two or three years ago, we would not have been faced with the introduction of Bill C-84.
Bill C-84 is unnecessary within the context of the clear message that a fast refugee determination policy would itself have been the most significant possible deterrent to abuse. A process which can take up to five years is a process subject to abuse. It creates the opportunity to come here to work, to establish one's self, to be even in a position to cast one's self before the mercy of the Government in order to remain in Canada in spite of the illegitimacy of the claim proffered.
This long process told people, come on over. You may not be a legitimate refugee but you can stay here for five years. Canada is a humane country, it is run by people who are
Immigration Act, 1976
empathic, so if these refugees manage to get here, the chances are pretty good they would be able to stay. That is self-evident.
Instead of dealing with this, we waited until public pressure mounted. Now we have entered into a debate, and many of the utterances I have heard in this debate have been shameful I sat here last week and listened to many Members on the Government side speak without shame. They laughed and hooted. They said things that would have depressed me enormously had I for one moment thought they were reflective of the views of the Canadian people.
1 stood in this House not too long ago and expressed pride in this country. It is a country which had begun the process of evolving into a model, showing the rest of the world how many peoples of different origins can live together to create a new society, a society devoted to social justice. In looking at Bill C-84 and Bill C-55 I reflected upon my own origins. I reflected upon the fact that, like many Canadians, my forbears came here as refugees. Indeed, my great, great-grandfather was one of those who brought 10 or more refugees into this country and not one of them had a document. Among those whom my great, great-grandfather brought to this country-his name being McCurdy-were the great-grandparents of my grandmother. They were slaves. They were refugees from slavery.
This country has changed a great deal. I reviewed my own history and thought of how my people have seen this country change. It was for that reason, at least in part, that I spoke with such pride about this country when I referred to the Nansen Medal. Having said that, 1 think it is the greatest weakness of politicians to behave opportunistically in response to a real crisis. There is no other way of regarding Bill C-55 and its twin. Bill C-84, except as pieces of legislation motivated primarily by opportunism, coloured so fundamentally by the opportunistic approach as to give offence to the new Canada. I sense a conflict between the senior Minister and the junior Minister. I know that the junior Minister is a man sympathetic to some of the things I have said this morning. Yet the Government has closed its ears to what has been universally regarded as a fair refugee determination process, that

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Resuming debate, the Hon. Member for Quebec-Est (Mr. Tremblay).
[ Translation]

Madam Speaker, we are gathered here today because the problem of aliens entering Canada illegally by claiming to be refugees has become an extremely serious one. The Canadian people are aware of this and the Government as well.
When the Government announced its intention to recall the House, it was accused of either over-reacting or being irresponsible. Doing nothing now would have been telling the world that Canada allows its laws to be broken. Doing nothing would have aggravated the dissension reflected in public opinion and thus put our programs for refugees and immigrants in jeopardy.
There is no doubt that Canada's humanitarian tradition of dealing with refugees may come to an end if we do not put a stop to the abuse being made of our system.
The Canadian people want measures to be introduced now, and we are going to do that.
The House was recalled for a specific task. We must stem the increasing flow of migrants arriving in Canada. We must put a stop to the organized and systematic abuse of our system for determining refugee status. We must take measures to put a stop to the exploitation of human misery by people who could be qualified as refugee traffickers.
Bill C-55 will introduce both fairness and control to the refugee determination process. It is the ultimate step in our plan of action to deal with a problem that has international implications. For most Canadians the dramatic arrival of 155 Tamils in Newfoundland one year ago was their first inkling that we have a refugee problem. That is not surprising when one considers that just six years ago only 1,600 people came to Canada claiming refugee status.
However, by 1986 the number had swelled to 18,000. This year we expect that it will reach 30,000.
More important than sheer numbers is the fact that many of these claims are not genuine. Our studies show that last year 70 per cent of refugee claimants were not refugees at all, and that many others had already found safe haven elsewhere before seeking refugee status in our country. The arrival of the Tamils reinforced our resolve to take action to stem the flow of phoney refugees. Quick action was necessary because of wide media interest in the Tamil boat people. The predictable happened-more and more illegal aliens poured into Canada.
We acted by improving measures to curb the flow of illegals to our shores. The control measures we introduced in February had a limited impact. Refugee claimant numbers which were averaging 1,200 a week in February have dropped to 500 a week today.

August 17, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
The control measures and the expanded powers that we are now seeking will deal effectively with short-term solutions to the refugee problem. But a long-term solution will only be found through the passage into law of Bill C-55.
And now for the problems we are having today. Madam Speaker, everyone knows why we have been called to this place, but I would like to repeat this for the benefit of certain opposition Members who seem to have forgotten already. It is because of a system already overloaded by a backlog of applications which is being exploited by queue-jumpers who are not legitimate refugees in need of our protection.
Unscrupulous racketeers are also taking advantage of the situation and misleading men and women into believing that they will be able to get them the papers required to gain admission to Canada. These racketeers bring these people to Canada under conditions which are often intolerable, unacceptable even for animals, and absolutely shocking in the case of human beings. Legitimate refugees suffer from delays in the system and are put at a disadvantage because of the increasing number and cleverness of fraudulent claims. Mr. Speaker, Canadians are getting more and more concerned about the inequity of the present system, which they believe to be incapable of these abuses. The patience of even the most generous and humanitarian Canadians is running out, and this Hon. Member, Madam Speaker, sees himself as a very tolerant person. Too many people enter Canada without the required documents and constitute a threat to our security.
We are certainly faced with a series of potentially explosive conditions which the Canadian people and the Government cannot accept. The situation requires that the Government take the required action. We are determined to put a stop to this traffic in human beings.
I also believe it important to throw some light on another major component of this Bill. The purpose of the proposed changes is not to discourage legitimate refugees who need our protection.
Bill C-55, combined with the other measures we have taken, will enable us to protect legitimate refugees.
With this Bill, we can develop a fairer, faster and more effective refugee determination system which will benefit all legitimate refugees. This system will respect the basic rights of all those who are entitled to claim refugee status.
Bill C-55 contains key provisions which will simplify the processing of claims, ensure faster rejection of unfounded claims and strengthen the powers of the Government. This will allow the Government to send back to third countries those whose claims are unfounded while respecting their fundamental rights.
We hope that, this time, the urgency of taking action and the increasing pressures throughout the world will convince the
Opposition to be more objective about the importance of Bill C-55.
The temporary measures we imposed in February were indeed only temporary. Bill C-55 goes further. It provides the long term solution needed to solve this problem, and this solution is both fair and judicious.
This legislation allows us to regain control over our refugee determination system which past abuses have rendered ineffective.
This is a valid solution, Madam Speaker. The Bill clearly and concisely defines the new process, which 1 repeat will be an equitable one.
As I have already said, Madam Speaker, we are here to conclude work undertaken several months ago, and Bill C-55 and the Bill on detention and deterrence are the result of this work.
The two Bills complement each other. We must ensure that our system really can weed out abuse, while allowing refugee claimants to put their cases. These two Bills give us the assurance needed. They guarantee the rights of everyone, but will deter many of those swindlers.
The aim of these two Bills is to put in place a refugee determination system that is more fair, more expeditious and better for all genuine refugees.
I keep repeating myself, but 1 feel that with the position we are now taking we must repeat the good points, in order that we take time to reflect on what is really at stake in these two Bills.
So as 1 said, what we are looking for is a system that respects the basic rights of all potential refugee claimants.
Yes, we are strongly determined to guarantee the rights of all refugee claimants. But we also want to check abuse. The deterrence and detention provisions will go to the root of the problem and allow us to exercise necessary control.
1 would now like to deal briefly with this Government's firm commitment to help genuine refugees.
It is essential to understand fully that our commitment to help genuine refugees is stronger than ever. In fact, Bill C-55 is a measure that is in line with the traditional justice and the humanitarian tradition for which the Nansen Medal was awarded to the Canadian people by the United Nations' High Commissioner for Refugees-the first time ever it was awarded to a whole nation.
Let me also remind all Members in this House and the Canadian people that since we have been elected, this Government significantly increased the number of refugees selected in camps around the world. This year, we are taking charge of 12,000 refugees from those camps, and private groups of Canadians and also families are sponsoring some 5,000 more.
August 17, 1987

Canada has a long tradition of proving its humanitarian concern for genuine refugees who need its protection. The new determination process will uphold this tradition of commitment to true refugees.
Our commitment goes back a long way. It is an essential part of a policy which, since the Second World War, has brought some 500,000 refugees to Canada for resettlement, and which has helped thousands of others through special humanitarian measures.
On a per capita basis Canada's record of aid to refugees over the past few years has been second to none.
We provide refugee assistance under three specific formulas. First, direct financial assistance; second, the settlement in Canada of refugees selected outside this country; and protection given in Canada pursuant to a determination process carried out here. This three-prong approach is in line with the United Nations refugee policy.
For 1986-87, the Canadian Government set more than $170 million aside for refugee financial assistance. One third of these funds-over $66 million-was given to international humanitarian organizations like the Red Cross and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, or to various countries in the form of food assistance for refugees. The rest of this money has been earmarked for adjustment assistance and language training for refugees selected abroad and for assistance to groups helping refugees to settle in Canada and become integrated in Canadian society.
Furthermore, refugees may obtain interest-free loans from the Government to finance the cost of their transportation to Canada.
The second part of the refugee program is resettlement of refugees selected abroad. In 1986, two-thirds of this group received Government assistance.
Groups consisting of private individuals and volunteer organizations sponsored over 5,000 more refugees. In such cases, the Government helps to match sponsors with refugees and offers the latter group transportation loans, language training and occupational training.
I would like to stress that many of the people admitted to Canada because they were selected abroad under this program do not necessarily meet the strict definition of refugee as defined in the Geneva Convention.
Canada has also developed some unique ways of helping victims of oppression, even if they do not meet the UN definition because they are still residing in their own country, for instance, political prisoners and other displaced persons in Poland, El Salvador, Guatemala, Chili and Uruguay.
We also help displaced persons who are in a situation similar to that of refugees, even if they do not meet the Convention definition. For instance, we have helped many people from Indo-China and Eastern Europe. In this case, we are dealing
Immigration Act, 1976
with people who, having left their countries of origin, did not manage to resettle permanently in another country.
Our purpose in introducing Bill C-55 was to make our refugee determination process efficient again, because this third part of our refugee program was simply not working.
At the present time, this process no longer makes it possible for us to extend our protection to the true refugees who need it because they can no longer sustain the pressure resulting from the enormous increase in the number of claims.
Through the proposed process, Canada will be able to continue fulfilling its obligations under the Geneva Convention while respecting the principles of justice which are the very foundation of our laws. Thus, we will be able to maintain our humanitarian tradition. We do not intend at all to turn our backs on refugees by adopting Bill C-55. Quite the contrary. We want to be able to extend a true protection to those who really need our help.
However, if we really seek to protect bona fide refugees, we must put an end to the abuse and reorganize the whole process.
When I deal with the policy of Canada towards refugees, I do so with considerable pride. Our refugee programs compare favourably with those of any country in the world. Our commitment to refugees is recognized internationally and the resettlement of refugees from camps abroad represents our most important contribution. A great many people have been stuck in camps for years without any alternative choice.
I suggest we must do the utmost to ensure that our tradition is maintained. But in order to do that, the refugee determination process must be changed. Canadians no longer can tolerate the current situation. They want a new refugee process that is both fair and tough to abusers.
As evidence of this, let me bring to your attention the results of a radio survey made in the Quebec area on August 3, 1987. The question was: Do you feel the Minister of Employment and Immigration, Hon. Benoit Bouchard, is right in proposing a tougher act to deny entry to refugees into Canada? Here is the response of citizens in that beautiful and great Quebec area-98 percent of the people supported those legislative measures. Two percent only opposed it. I was told the number of calls to that radio survey was larger than average, and according to the station's management, it was the most decisive in the history of their surveys.
I submit, that the people have spoken their minds, and as a responsible Government we have a duty to listen and act according to the people's will. We have the solution to that problem-now is the time to refer Bill C-55 to committee for review. Enough speeches, and I conclude on this, the time has come to act.

comments. The Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi).

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask my colleague two very quick questions because 1 know other Hon. Members wish to comment on the speech he has just made.
First, the Hon. Member said that his Government was awarded the Nansen Medal. Would he not wish to clarify that for the record by saying that in fact the Government certainly did not win that award for its achievements over the last two years, but that the Nansen Medal was awarded for the very first time to a country for a record that had been demonstrated over years gone by when his Party was still on this side of the House? 1 think the Hon. Member should have the honesty to clarify that.
Second, the Hon. Member went on at some length suggesting that Bills C-55 and C-84 somehow meet with the approval of the Geneva Convention to which we were a signatory in 1969. Having said that, would he care to comment on what he thinks about the letter that was released last Friday by the United Nations High Commissioner who, despite couching his remarks in very diplomatic language, expressed clear concern for the direction the Government was taking? If in fact the Government does not wish to uphold the United Nations Charter, why is it not prepared to tell Canadians that it is no longer prepared to live with that agreement, rather than doing it through a sneaky, back-handed, back-door approach?

Madam Speaker, 1 will answer the two questions very briefly. On the first one, I mentioned in my speech that the Canadian Government indeed had the privilege to receive the Nansen Award, and as a Canadian I am very proud of that.
On the second question, after much reading on the matter and articulating Bills C-84 and C-55, which complement each other, it is my view that everything that has been written and said by this Goverment had but one goal-to protect all Canadians without exception, and to some extent I admire the Opposition. It cannot always be easy to get mentally prepared to criticize proposals which are so obvious, since they are fair and equitable. They deserve some credit for that and I am aware of it.

Madam Speaker, most Canadians would agree with the suggestion of the Hon. Member that we want a refugee system that is humane, fair and quick. How can the Hon. Member say that the Bills that are before us will provide for such a system, when on June 1 of this year a telex was sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) signed by and on behalf of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, the Anglican
Church, the Canadian Baptist Federation, the Canadian Council of Churches, the Council of Christian Reform Churches, the Mennonite Central Committee, the Presbyterian Church of Canada, the Salvation Army, the Quakers, the United Church of Canada and the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees making it very clear to the Prime Minister and the Government that in the view of these organizations, which certainly have no political axe to grind, the legislation was very deficient?
Second, why did the Government not follow the recommendations made by the Standing Committee which dealt with this question in great depth? This committee had a large majority of government members on it. It issued a unanimous report making very specific recommendations, most of which were not included in this legislation.

Madam Speaker, I am happy to reply to the question raised by my colleague for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). I would remind him of a poll to which I have already referred. The question asked to the residents of the beautiful region of Quebec City was this: Do you believe that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) is right to propose harsher legislation to refuse refugees entry into Canada? Of all those canvassed, 98 per cent said yes. But what if the question had been phrased this way: Do you believe that the Minister of Employment and Immigration is right to propose harsher legislation to refuse entry to fradulent refugees? I believe that 150 per cent of respondents would have said yes. This is a recent poll and the results are clear. They represent a diversified segment of the population of my region. There are all kinds of happy people in that region. This is what the people think. Many of these respondents are from my own constituency. I have always been very receptive to their comments, and this poll, has shown me what I must do.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 have a question for the Hon. Member for Quebec East (Mr. Tremblay). The main strength of Bill C-55 is certainly that it will help to reduce the delays in processing refugee claims. It contains provisions which will allow the authorities to process claims more quickly than in the past, and I believe that everyone agrees with that. We are not here to discuss whether or not Canada needs refugees. We have always welcomed them in the past.
Bills C-55 and C-84 deal with illegal or irregular claimants and abusers of the system. One of the provisions of Bill C-55 concerns that new concept. That is one of the weaknesses of the Bill.
The new concept advocated is that the Government or Cabinet will establish a list of so-called safe countries about which we will be able to say: "In that country there is no danger of violence against basic freedoms". The Cabinet will have to establish a list of safe countries, the concept of the safe third country.
August 17, 1987

1 have a question for the Hon. Member, because we all know such a list will create problems. The Cabinet has always refrained from establishing this kind of list because it is not easy to politicize the whole process and make such momentous decisions.
The question is this: For example, the United States do not accept refugees from Guatemala, they do not accept immigrants from other countries, 1 could name some, San Salvador for one, they send them back home.
The federal Cabinet will have to decide whether the United States is a third safe country. Is it really a country where we can send a refugee or so-called refugee arriving in Canada, under the pretense that he will be well there and not be threatened?
We all know that the policy of the Americans is to send home people arriving from San Salvador and Guatemala.
How can the Hon. Member reconcile this question of the safe third country, knowing full well that we are on very good terms with the Americans but have serious reasons to believe that an individual might come from Guatemala or San Salvador and tell us: "My personal safety is threatened or I am otherwise threatened with respect to expressing my basic freedom". Would the Hon. Member tell us how he would deal with that problem, how he would respond to this refugee whose personal and individual rights are threatened?

Madam Speaker, I should think that Canadian representatives and Canadian embassies throughout the world have enough experience and credibility to be aware of what is going on every day, and to be in a position to have an updated list of what we call "safe countries".
So far the Cabinet has demonstrated that we ought to have confidence in them and 1 would leave any such decision up to them.

Madam Speaker, Bill C-55 is a strange and inadequate response to the very serious need for a review not only of refugee policy but of immigration policy in general. Since this Bill and Bill C-8'4 deal with refugee policy and not other aspects of immigration, I will confine my remarks to that.
1 was chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration in 1976 when we passed an immigration Bill. At that time immigration law had not been updated for about 20 years. The Department of Immigration was running along on volumes and volumes of ministerial directives and regulations. The law was then updated and it was quite clear that with the changing issues in immigration there should be a further updating well before another 20 years had passed.
Immigration Act, 1976
The refugee policy passed at that time did not provide for automatic oral hearings. There was a very elaborate paper screening effort and people had oral hearings later on in the determination process. It became clear this was causing problems.
I spoke in this House in March, 1984, on a motion recommending that all refugee applicants have oral hearings. I supported the motion for two reasons. First, an oral hearing early on in the process could result in faster decisions, and would enable the genuine refugee to know where he or she stood so that they could get on with having trade and professional qualifications evaluated and establishing a life in Canada. It would also screen out the bogus refugees who were starting to appear even at that time.
The second reason I was in favour of oral hearings early on was that I was sure members of the Refugee Status Advisory Committee, as it was called at that time, as they examined sworn statements, must sometimes encounter doubts which could be resolved by a simple question or brief conversation with the claimant. I also said that our refugee policies and practices should be subject to ongoing review.
I think there were some principles held at that time which still hold today and on which we can agree. First, that Canada's effort in formulating and administering refugee policy is an essential reflection of Canada's humanitarian interests. Canadians have shown they have the capacity to reach out to those who are suffering persecution for reasons of race, religion, or politics, and to give comfort to the homeless and stateless. We have demonstrated a concern that our institutions and administrative practices reflect those humanitarian ideals. However, as I said then, and as I repeat today, we also have to exercise those instincts and goals, keeping in mind the protection of the best interests of Canada and of ensuring over-all fairness in our immigration policies.
Unlike other countries, Canada has not in the past faced a situation where large numbers of people claiming refugee status arrived at our borders. We are protected by three oceans. However, air travel has changed that. We are living in a time when strife and civil unrest are common. We are also living in difficult economic times. It is estimated that at any moment in time now some 70 million to 80 million people are on the move. Some are genuine refugees according to the UN standard. Some are unhappy, desperate people moving because of war, revolution and poverty. Some have the same motivation that immigrants have, the desire to create a better life and future for themselves and their children.
Where does Canada stand in all this? What are our obligations both to our citizens and those who wish to come to Canada? Clearly we cannot accommodate 70 million to 80 million people.

August 17, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
When 1 was a delegate to the UN in 1980 there was a lot of discussion, as there has been since, on the need to find better ways to settle refugees nearer their own homes and the need to find better methods of dispute settlement, protection of human rights, and of ensuring economic prosperity in third world countries. Those all form very basic parts of any approach to refugees and 1 have not heard any discussion of that kind in this debate. The Government's response to the present situation is simply to find ways of slamming the doors on refugees, keeping them off our shores. That does not touch on the international problem.
We have before us two Bills which are primarily designed to deal with abuses. They do not take a constructive approach to the real situation of refugees. When 1 spoke in March, 1984, in favour of oral hearings, I said that Canada was then averaging about 500 applicants for refugee status per month, that this was double the number in the previous year, 1983, and that about 9,500 cases were under review for appeal yet only one-third of those who claimed refugee status had their claims upheld.
Those numbers have since exploded. 1 understand that the number of refugee applicants in the first six months of 1987 approached 16,000 and that only about 10 per cent of those who applied were determined to be refugees. Therefore, the numbers are significantly different and a response on the part of the Government is needed. However, the response is not Bill C-55 or Bill C-84.
Part of the reason for the flood of refugee applicants is, of course, the activities of so-called immigration consultants and of certain lawyers specializing in immigration. In my constituency at one time there were five people operating. Four of them were not lawyers while one was, and he, 1 believe, has since been charged. There is another lawyer who has not been charged and who, to the best of my knowledge, has never advocated any actually illegal proceeding. However, he certainly takes on hopeless immigration cases at 53,000 a go. My constituents ask me what the difference is between him and a consultant who charges $1,500 to advise someone to tell a few lies at an immigration hearing.
There is an appalling traffic in human misery. Some of the people who want to immigrate to Canada, although not refugees by the UN standard, are trying to escape difficult, painful situations which we can only imagine. It is absolutely appalling that they are being preyed upon and trafficked in by people who are escaping scott-free.
For this I have to be very critical of the Government. The Minister and his officials have certainly known of the activities of these so-called consultants and less than scrupulous lawyers for well over two years. We have seen nothing but inaction. There are measures in the present legislation which would have allowed action to be taken. Remarkably little has been done. The extraordinary and Draconian legislation now before
us was not necessary because there are powers in the existing legislation to deal with the problems. There are powers contained within the Criminal Code to deal with fraud which have not been used.
The Minister's officials know, as well as I, that there is a lively traffic in social insurance number cards, that ineligible people are working on building sites all over Toronto. There are remarkably young, healthy men carrying cards which belong to 65 year-olds. This has been well known for a long time and no action has been taken. The Minister's officials know which union halls ask no questions but will send anyone out to a job without the production of identification and proof that he has status in the country. Nothing has been done.
For the Government, which has not taken action, which has not used the existing provisions in the law against fraud, to in effect say that the whole refugee process is so fraudulent that we need Draconian legislation to stop all refugee applicants at the border is surely to attack the problem in the wrong place.
I hope that the news we heard today is not true. There is a report in the newspapers that the Minister is seriously considering building some kind of fortress to house 2,500 refugee applicants. We will wait with interest to see what the Minister has to say about that, whether he will claim that he was misquoted.
Section 95(n) of the present Immigration Act allows prosecution of those who would counsel or assist illegal immigrants. That section has not been used other than to prosecute the captain of the Amelie. In other cases the most extraordinary abuses are taking place and the Government remains inactive.
To repeat, I know that Canadians want us to have a just, humane refugee policy. Canadians want genuine refugees to be admitted. Our past experience has been that they become very good citizens. One example is the 160,000 boat people from Vietnam who were settled in Canada with the aid and active involvement of many Canadian citizens and church groups who participated with the Government in providing sponsorship and offering friendship and assistance to families.
Canadian generosity has not changed. However, Canadians certainly do not want to see scams. Canadians do not want to have the system abused. That is abusive to our own taxpayers and also to genuine refugees. Canadians want abuses stopped. However, the two Bills before us are not designed to stop abuses but to close the door to genuine refugees. That is why I have to oppose them.
Mir. Friesen: Madam Speaker, I listened with care to the Hon. Member's speech. I always find it useful to hear what she has to say. She said that there was urgency to deal with fraud and fraudulent cases. Would she then tell us whether she thinks it is reasonable to delay this legislation for another six months and pass it in 1988, as indicated in the amendment to which we are now speaking?
August 17, 1987

Madam Speaker, as I pointed out, this Bill does not address the question of fraud. There are provisions in the existing Immigration Act to deal with fraud, which provisions have not been used by the Government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Madam Speaker, would the Member not agree that when groups of so-called refugees, which may indeed be refugees, arrive in numbers large enough to knowingly plug up the system, that is a kind of fraud which destroys the system?

Madam Speaker, the reason that fraudulent applicants can plug up the system is because the system is in need of revision. The Government added to that problem by announcing last year an amnesty, which it called by another name. At the time it was announced, that in itself triggered a tremendous amount of activity on the part of so-called consultants who were advertising in papers all over the world. There was a very deliberate attempt to plug up the system at that time and the Government should have foreseen it. It created the problem about which it is now complaining.
