Mr. Speaker, Canadians across this land have been telling the Conservative Government for the last three years that we need an affordable, accessible and comprehensive quality child care system. They said it through the Abella Report, the Cooke Task Force, the "Equality for AH" report and the recently tabled Martin report.
Child care has been described as the basic building block to access and equality of opportunity in the workforce for mothers. While this is a most serious consideration, even more important is ignoring the scarcity of services that neglects the real beneficiaries of child care, our children.
Whether pre-school or latch key for after school care, children need the protection and benefits of such a system whenever the absence of the parents requires an alternate form of care.
The Conservatives have had the time and opportunity to establish the needed federal position on child care. How can Canadians trust the Government's political will when it gives nothing but excuses, platitudes and a one-and-a-half page farcical letter as answer to this major social issue? It is time for action for the mothers, fathers and children of our land.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR MEASURES TO PREVENT ABUSES OF SYSTEM
SUPPORT FOR MEASURES TO PREVENT ABUSES OF SYSTEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, queue jumping by potential new Canadians to get into our country is simply not acceptable. Canada cannot and should not tolerate unscrupulous persons from anywhere who deal in human flesh at our borders at the expense of legitimate individuals who are waiting abroad to follow standard immigration procedures. Nor should we admit illegal refugees to our lands.
The vast majority of Canadians, almost 80 per cent, support the current Government's actions, and over 60 per cent said we should have gone further. Canadians are obviously in a mood for new tough measures to deal with immigration problems.
Canada can and should continue to welcome new persons to its shores. As we all know, our country has the capacity to do so, but not at the expense of those who are honestly trying to come here. Hundreds of my constituents, many of whom are new Canadians, have told me we should be firm, fair, quick and tough on illegal and unfair practices. I believe we are.

subtopic: REPORTED PLAN TO CONSTRUCT DETENTION CENTRE
REPORTED PLAN TO CONSTRUCT DETENTION CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the media report that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) is planning a detention centre for 2,500 refugee claimants. This would be a horrible throwback to 45 years ago when our Government imprisoned 22,000 permanent residents of Canada, mostly Canadian born, and stripped them of nearly all their property solely because of their racial origin.
Unnecessary detention is cruel and such large scale detentions are not needed to protect Canada from refugees. The ancient people of Israel, although they suffered many attacks by enemies and many invasions, nevertheless made it a law to protect strangers who came in peace and unarmed. Jesus promised the kingdom to those who welcomed him in the person of a stranger.
I urge the Minister to drop this idea and cancel any tenders he may have called for the construction of such a cruel detention centre.

August 17, 1987

Mr. Speaker, Canada's honey industry has been plagued with more than its share of problems this past couple of years. I won't go into all the horrid details, but weather, disease, management as a result of poor advice, and honey prices are some of the complications. If something is not done soon to straighten out these problems the industry will be in serious trouble.
Financial problems are created by the United States Farm Support Bill which in turn does not bring a viable price to the Canadian producer. Honey was not on the list of commodities covered by the special grains payment made to Canadian farmers.
The honey industry has been a self-sufficient industry until recently and I call upon our Government to hurry up with the support for which the Canadian Honey Council has made application.

subtopic: PROPOSED TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM THROUGH CANADIAN AIRSPACE
PROPOSED TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM THROUGH CANADIAN AIRSPACE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next month the United States and Japan are expected to ratify an agreement to ship plutonium from Europe to Japan through Canadian air space. By allowing these overflights of plutonium Canada would jeopardize human life, caribou, polar bears and other forms of life should an accident take place.
The inhalation of toxic plutonium dust leads to slow death by cancer. The people in Yellowknife and perhaps even Edmonton could conceivably be at risk depending on wind direction, location of the crash site and the extent of destruction to the plutonium carrying casks.
The quantity of plutonium to be shipped means two flights per month for 30 years. If one overflight is allowed it will be difficult to stop the second, third, or three hundredth.
I urge the Government to notify the United States and Japan now, before the signing of the agreement in mid-September, and make it known that the Government of Canada is opposed to the transport of plutonium over its territory, and therefore avoid any risks to people, property and the environment. What Canadians want from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) is reassurance and preventive action.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR PASSAGE OF LEGISLATION AMENDING PATENT ACT
SUPPORT FOR PASSAGE OF LEGISLATION AMENDING PATENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr Speaker, I would like to draw to the attention of the House the numerous tfelegrams and letters I have received from my constituents urging me to support the passage of Bill C-22 as presented by the Minister.
Around the world the creation of new ideas and inventions is protected by copyrights and patents, that is everywhere but here in Canada. Canada stands alone among the industrialized countries in imposing compulsory licensing when a company obtains a patent for a new drug. This means that anyone else can copy that drug as long as it pays a 4 per cent royalty. That is legal piracy, the stealing of a company's intellectual property. It has to stop.
Bill C-22 will allow people and companies to do research with their time and with their money here in Canada. One really has to wonder if Senators have considered that the drug companies involved have promised Canada approximately $900 million in spending on research and development and the creation of 3,000 jobs for Canadians.

subtopic: SHORTAGES EXPERIENCED BY MUNICIPAL FOOD BANKS
SHORTAGES EXPERIENCED BY MUNICIPAL FOOD BANKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in recent months there has been a dramatic increase in the number of people who visit food banks in every part of Canada and in every city and town. These are food banks which have been established by voluntary agencies. For the first time there are skilled workers who have lost their jobs and executives of middle management from major companies who are finding it impossible to continue without the help of these food banks.
This summer many alarms have been sounded as community food banks have run short of enough supplies to feed the hungry. Huge shortages have been reported in big cities such as Toronto, and in smaller cities such as Kingston. Provinces such as Alberta and now British Columbia have compounded the difficulties by reducing welfare rates.
We have to ask ourselves how much longer it will be before food banks begin to crack because of the intense pressures caused by Governments which no longer care enough to help. Already cities such as Regina are turning to provincial and federal Governments to assist in a proposed universal school meal program to help feed that city's more than 2,000 hungry children each day.
August 17, 1987

When will the federal Government address the basic problems of hunger and malnutrition for so many Canadians? Some of us have been asking this same question for at least two years. It is time the Government got to work on what is a very important and serious problem.

subtopic: PATENT ACT AMENDMENTS-OPPOSITION OF NEW DEMOCRATIC AND LIBERAL PARTIES
PATENT ACT AMENDMENTS-OPPOSITION OF NEW DEMOCRATIC AND LIBERAL PARTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Liberals and New Democrats are strong on the rhetoric of research, development and productivity. But, in practice, they bend to the winds of political expediency opposing the Government's amendments to the Patent Act. Let the Opposition explain this to the 66 working men and women in the pharmaceutical industry in Arnprior who, out of concern for their jobs and their futures, sent telegrams to their Member of Parliament.
Let them explain to Canadians how, in their search for a few easy votes, they have opposed legislation which will encourage and reward those companies which dare to invest in research, developing drugs which ease human suffering and save lives.
Let the senatorial scaremongers try to explain to scientists and researchers across the country why they chose to call up the spectre of unreasonable fears rather than taking the tough decisions necessary to reward innovation and productivity.

subtopic: PROSPECT OF ELECTION OF A LIBERAL GOVERNMENT
PROSPECT OF ELECTION OF A LIBERAL GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this statement has no connection with the forthcoming election. That is how announcements regarding major projects in New Brunswick are prefaced.
On the week-end it was announced that $20 million would be added to the Canada-New Brunswick Agreement on Tourism. Wonderful! This means that projects previously turned down because of lack of funds will now be able to proceed.
We still do not know whether this announcement has any connection with the upcoming election campaign in New Brunswick. 1 don't think so. Let me explain.
Everybody in New Brunswick knows that the Hatfield Government is breathing its last. Everyboby knows that no agreement and no amount of money would be able to buy the New Brunswick election for the Hatfield team.
Mr. Speaker, 1 am sure that in his wisdom, the federal Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Valcourt) is aware that in New Brunswick, the die is cast, and whatever he does, he will not be able to influence the vote towards the present Government, which is so exhausted it doesn't even have the courage to call an election. The Minister is also aware that the next election in New Brunswick will lead to a Liberal landslide that will be remembered in history as the McKenna landslide.
Mr. Speaker, it is only a matter of time.

Mr. Speaker, sensible, thinking Canadians from every walk of life are appalled at the current refugee determination process whereby anyone can come to Canada at any time, by any means, from anywhere, and upon arrival refuse to identify themselves, and in the same breath claim all the rights and privileges of Canadian citizenship.
We are told that upwards of 500 refugee claimants are arriving weekly with virtually unlimited potential for more. Furthermore, 90 per cent of these claimants are bogus refugees, line jumpers who make a mockery of our laws and who proclaim to the world that Canada is an easy mark.
My constituents are saying that this is grossly unfair; surely, common sense must prevail. They congratulate the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) on bringing forward Bills C-84 and C-55 which will increase penalties against smugglers, and make it easier to detain refugee claimants. They urge speedy passage of these Bills.

subtopic: PAYMENT OF BENEFIT CONTRIBUTIONS DURING MATERNITY LEAVE
PAYMENT OF BENEFIT CONTRIBUTIONS DURING MATERNITY LEAVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the past I have brought up the issue of paid benefits for people who are on maternity leave. At that time I requested that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) act.
It is important to note that in September, 1985, the Government sent out a circular in the format of questions and answers. One of the questions was:
Is the employer required to continue benefit contributions while the
employee is on leave?

August 17, 1987
Oral Questions
The answer was:
Yes, bu! only if the employee also pays contributions he or she would normally have made.
That being the case, women assumed that they would have the normal benefits paid by the employer continue. Since then the Government has received a legal opinion which was sent out by James Allan from the Minister of Labour's office. In that letter it states:
We now have a final opinion from legal services. They advise that Section 59.52 does not obligate an employer to pay their "usual" cost of benefits during maternity/child care leave. We are also advised that since there is no legal obligation for employers to pay, a prosecution under the Code would probably not succeed.
I ask that the Minister of Labour live up to the obligations of his Department, of the House of Commons, and of the law as it was passed in 1984, and make appropriate changes to the Canada Labour Code to ensure that women on maternity leave receive paid benefits.
* *
*

subtopic: REFUGEE DETERMINATION SYSTEM ABUSES-SUPPORT FOR AMENDING LEGISLATION
REFUGEE DETERMINATION SYSTEM ABUSES-SUPPORT FOR AMENDING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the end of World War 11, hundreds of thousands of refugees have come to our country, usually after being processed by Canadian officials in one of the many refugee camps around the world. Until recently, only a handful arrived in Canada and then claimed refugee status. That has jumped dramatically, from 1,600 in 1980 to over 18,000 last year. This is partly due to the increase in the world's refugee population, which is presently estimated to be at least 12 million. However, 70 per cent of those who arrive here and then claim refugee status are queue jumpers, posing as refugees to gain quick entrance into Canada.
Canadians do not like queue jumpers. Rightly so, they feel it is unfair to immigrants waiting to come into our country legally. Bills C-84 and C-55 are not aimed at genuine refugees. They are aimed at deterring queue jumpers, and at fairness for immigrant applicants who want to play by the rules. That is what Canadians really want.
* *
*

subtopic: NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL OPPOSING POSITION OF SENATE IN AMENDING PATENT ACT LEGISLATION

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
subtopic: NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL OPPOSING POSITION OF SENATE IN AMENDING PATENT ACT LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to take this opportunity to quote from The Packet
& Times editorial on August 1 5, 1987. The editorial is entitled "Drug patent bill-obstructionism by Senate". It states:
In opposing the federal governments' proposed new drug patent bill, the Senate is staging a grandstand play. We hope Canadians will not be fooled by it.
At present, in Canada, genetic drug companies are allowed to make cheap copies of medications developed by major drug companies in return for a mere 4 per cent royalty.
Canada is the only country in the western world which allows this piracy. Most protect the drug investors for 10 years or, in some cases, much longer.
Canada's practice is unfair. If we treated other "inventors'' in such manner we wouldn't have any new inventions.
If we expect the major drug companies to spend the billions of dollars required to develop new medications ... for the benefit of us all... we must offer some protection ...
The Senate, in a deliberate attempt at obstruction, has revised the legislation calling for... a four-year monopoly.
The Liberal-dominated Senate claims that in proposing the law, the Mulroney government is bending to the demands of the U.S. government and drug company lobbyists.
This ignores the fact that European drug companies and other governments are as much upset at our piracy as the Americans.
I call upon the other place to abandon its obstruction.

subtopic: NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL SUPPORTING POSITION OF SENATE IN AMENDING PATENT ACT LEGISLATION
NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL SUPPORTING POSITION OF SENATE IN AMENDING PATENT ACT LEGISLATION

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-FUTURE OF AUTO PACT

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-FUTURE OF AUTO PACT

August 17, 1987

Oral Questions
We do not want to know the negotiating position of the Government and we do not want to know how the Government will play its cards. However, we do want to know what cards are in the deck, those items that are negotiable and on the table with the United States.
1 could cite to the right hon. gentleman a statement made on regional subsidies. The Minister said on March 16 that regional development and our capacity to sustain regional development are not on the table. Five paragraphs later, she said also on the table are subsidies and related measures which are important to regional development because we want to know what programs we will be able to implement for regional development.
That is a perfect example of the lack of clarity of the Minister and it is for that reason that 1 ask the Right Hon. Member this question: are regional subsidies, those elements of Canadian national policy necessary to achieve economic equality across Canada, part of the negotiations with the United States, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, what is being talked about here is a trade negotiation. Now he seems to have a new proposal and that new proposal is that since the Government is determined to follow the advice of, among, others the Liberal Premier of the Province of Quebec, by proceeding with the best efforts attempt to negotiate a trade arrangement, he is trying to ask us to act in a way that would put the Canadian case on the table for the advantage of the Americans in a way that would destroy the Canadian case. That is not the way we will proceed with these negotiations.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with that type of answer there will be no overwhelming demand that the Minister stay in the country for any length of time.
The Right Hon. Member's colleague and Leader, the Prime Minister, admitted last week that the drug legislation, Bill C-22 shortly to be before the House, has been discussed with the Americans. It took a little prodding, but we got that admission. Since the Americans have always contended that the drug legislation is a matter for negotiation in free trade with Canada, has the Government consulted recently with the

August 17, 1987
Oral Questions
Americans to ascertain whether the compromise set forth in the Eastman report would be a position acceptable to the Americans?

Mr. Speaker, what an amazing attempt to give away Canada's sovereignty. We make those decisions here in Canada, we do not ask the United States to make those kinds of decisions.
The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition has asked a question based upon discussions with other Governments regarding Bill C-22. 1 can tell him that I have heard from other Governments about the situation of piracy that is the law of Canada now which we are trying to change. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: BILL C-84-UNITED NATIONS CONVENTION ON REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Immigration. Last Friday in response to a question put by my Leader, he suggested that under Bill C-84 we will not violate our international obligations. However, we have since learned that in a letter dated August 12 sent to the Government of Canada, the United Nations High Commissioner on Refugees expressed grave concern with the policy of the Government and in the process delivered an international slap in the face to Canada which was heard the world over.
Knowing our precise commitments to the United Nations and having received a letter prior to the commencement of the emergency debate last week, why did the Minister persist in misleading the House and Canadians into believing that the United Nations Convention is not being breached by Bill C-84? Will the Minister make the necessary amendments so that Canada can save face with the United Nations? In that regard, what instructions have been sent to Ambassador Stephen Lewis?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: BILL C-84-UNITED NATIONS CONVENTION ON REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 received the comments of the United Nations High Commissioner and I responded to those comments in a letter last week. 1 am confident my explanation will satisfy the concerns of the High Commissioner.
In the letter 1 said that the powers permitted to states by Article 25 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea authorizes the denial of entry and the enforced departure of vehicles from territorial waters where there is reason to believe those vehicles are transporting a person or persons to Canada in contravention of the Immigration Act or regulations. The Bill requires the Minister to exercise due regard to the safety of the vehicle and the passengers before giving the direction to depart. This provides ample opportunity for the Minister to take into account a variety of considerations before making his decision.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister should know that the UN Commissioner is not stupid. His concern is for the safety of refugees. We are squandering the international leadership role on which Canadians have prided themselves. We are losing sovereignty at home, respect abroad, so what else is left?
You!

Bill C-84 will render our signature to the UN Convention on Refugees null and void as was diplomatically implied by the UN Commissioner. Why does the Government not have the honesty and integrity to tell Canadians and this House very clearly that it no longer believes in the UN Convention, that it is pulling Canada out of that convention, rather than trying to do it through a sneaky back door approach? You cannot have it both ways. Which one is it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share the opinion of my colleague that the High Commissioner for Refugees is certainly not a stupid person, and this is why we responded at length to the question he asked us. I am sincerely convinced that the High Commissioner for Refugees will accept Canada's argument with respect to dissuading bogus refugees from resorting to illegal means to enter this country. We reserve the right to send back ships caught in international waters, but again with every assurance that in the case of people sent back, if ever this should happen, we will have given consideration to the safety aspects and made sure that neither the life nor the future of such individuals would be compromised in any way whatsoever.
August 17, 1987

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF NEGOTIATING END TO APARTHEID-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Secretary of State was quoted as saying that he has come back from South Africa with practical proposals to negotiate an end to apartheid. This seems to be a major development. Can the Secretary of State tell the House what these proposals are?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF NEGOTIATING END TO APARTHEID-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are no specific proposals and 1 regret having been misquoted. Some developments have come to light in my discussions with the African National Congress and the government of South Africa which are minimally encouraging. I must say that, as far as negotiations are concerned, 1 do not believe that there can be any major progress in the forseeable future, but there have been some elements of agreement between the two parties which hold some hope for the future. For instance, both parties have indicated that they would prefer a negotiated solution to one achieved through violence. Both have indicated that, in their opinion, if the apartheid issue is settled by violent means in South Africa, it will have terrible consequences for everyone in the region, both Black and White.
Third, and 1 believe that this is very important, the ANC recognizes that it is not the only group representing South African Blacks that must be involved in any negotiations. Finally, neither the government of South Africa nor the ANC have closed the door on future negotiations.

Mr. Speaker, quite evidently the visit of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to South Africa was intended as a preparation for both the Francophone Summit and the Commonwealth Summit.
In view of the experiences of the Secretary of State in southern Africa, is it the intention of the Government to bring forth any specific propositions at all to those two conferences? Quite specifically, is it the intention of the Government to fulfil its promise to try to agree to new sanctions by those two bodies in view of the lack of change in southern Africa?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will have the privilege later today of being present when the Prime Minister meets the Secretary General of the Commonwealth, Mr. Ramphal, at which time there will be discussion of some of the matters which will come
Oral Questions
to the agenda of the Commonwealth Conference. Many of those will concern South Africa.
Although that conference is also dealing with a wider world and a wider range of issues, there are some specific proposals that will be considered. If those proposals are to have effect, they have to become subject to the agreement of all of the members of the Commonwealth there assembled. I frankly do not think they would benefit from publication here at this time.
1 received some suggestions during my visit, not only from Governments but also from, among others, Reverend Alan Boesak, that may provide some opportunity for action by the Commonwealth. We will study that very seriously.
With regard to the question of sanctions, I think it should be borne in mind that sanctions are one instrument of encouraging change and that there are others.
1 think it important to make the point, immediately after my return to Canada, that had the Prime Minister, the Government and I accepted, two years ago, the advice of some in this House that we rupture entirely at that time our relations with South Africa, Canada would not have been in a position to have had the discussions which I was able to hold. We would not have been in a position to put to work the unique credibility of Canada as a country which might be able to build some kind of bridge across which agreement between the ANC and the South African Government might move.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, surely the credibility of the Government and of the country is tested as much by the promise of the Prime Minister that diplomatic relations would be broken if there was not some amelioration of the situation under apartheid.
1 will direct my question to either the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State. It may not be that apartheid is the only issue at the Commonwealth, but it certainly is the most important. There is agreement that sanctions and other actions are necessary.
Is it not clear that unless some strong action is taken by Canada and the Commonwealth in response to apartheid in South Africa that in itself would pose a threat to the seriousness with which the Commonwealth is regarded by its membership?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I think that is the case. I think it is important that the Commonwealth act. However, taking an action is only part of the challenge. The other part of the challenge is that the action be appropriate.
I have discussed this matter in some detail recently with President Kaunda, who is not only the President of Zambia

August 17, 1987
Oral Questions
but also the Chairman of the Front Line States and the Chairman of the Organization of African Unity. I have discussed it with the leaders of the African National Congress. When the Prime Minister was in Africa himself in January he had the opportunity to discuss precisely these questions. We will continue to look for ways that will be effective.
If I may say so, part of the reason that we were able to have some small influence upon the possible elaboration of a possible negotiating position was because the Prime Minister has shown leadership on this issue which is recognized throughout Africa and, I think, throughout the developing world.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Transport I will direct my question to the Deputy Prime Minister. Airline deregulation in the United States has had a direct adverse effect on safety. The Detroit tragedy of yesterday may well be another terrible example of this situation.
Why is the Government not ready to do anything to prevent similar tragedies from occurring here in Canada after Canadian airline deregulation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course we all regret very much the very serious tragedy which took place in Detroit. I am sure all Canadians will mourn with the families and friends of those who perished. We extend to them the comfort and compassion of the people of Canada.
I find the Hon. Member's question quite irresponsible. This accident is being investigated by the National Transportation Safety Board. None of the facts has been determined. It involved an MD-80 aircraft which is a development of the DC-9. There are no such aircraft registered in Canada. The engines were a JT8D-200 engine which is a very much advanced engine. Northwest Airlines has an impressive record. 1 think that making that kind of allegation is totally uncalled for.
I simply want to assure Canadians and the House that one of the first things the Government did was to take extra precautions to tighten up on the safety regulations in the airline industry by passing a new Aeronautics Act which is the most progressive, advanced and far-reaching safety legislation of any country in the world. For the Hon. Member to tie politics to a very serious tragedy is most unfortunate indeed.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the
Minister's answer is not good enough. Does the Minister know that airline mechanical engineers are delegated powers by the Department of Transport in Canada and are put in charge of applying the standards laid down by the Canadian Department?
How can we have the companies policing themselves? This is unacceptable. I hope the Minister will be ready to change this practice.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall).

Madam Speaker, today I wish to address some of the arguments made by the opposition Members and certain vested interest groups who believe that the Government is over-reacting in proposing this refugee determination legislation. They believe that the refugee situation in Canada today is not that serious, and that it does not deserve our urgent attention. I do not know where our critics have been. In my riding this past weekend, and prior to the House being recalled, I have received numerous phone calls, letters, and representations in my four constituency offices, and here in Ottawa, which indicate that people firmly believe that the Government was proper in recalling the House to deal with these Bills.
I would like to lay before the House the notion that all Canadians are very concerned and interested in immigration, and that we as a Government deal with the Bills before us. Whether my colleagues across the floor will admit it or not, every Member of the House has heard from the public on this issue. The message coming through loud and clear is, we are mad as hell about flagrant abuses to our refugee determination system. We are not going to take it any longer. The Government has to do something, and do it now.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) should be applauded for coming forward in such a timely fashion with this take charge, take action legislation. Bills C-55 and C-84 will continue our long history of extending humanitarianism to those truly in need, while sending out a clear, uncompromising message to those who take advantage of our natural goodwill.
Around the world Canadians have the reputation of being good guys. From here on in, these "good guys" will not finish last when it comes to removing illegal immigrants, and stopping in their tracks the unscrupulous smugglers who traffic in human desperation.
The critics of this legislation lay the audacious charge that the Government does not care about the plight of refugees, and that the Government does not act on behalf of refugees. I welcome this opportunity to set the record straight and tell the House that the media and the Opposition have, by gross omission, left untold the many ongoing actions and financial outlays the Government has initiated to assist refugees around the world.
While the debate over the new refugee determination system focuses on refugee claims made within Canada, we must not forget that Canada offers protection to refugees through our overseas programs. In this way we have for years shared the responsibility for the international refugee situation. Each year we offer refugee status, transportation to Canada, and resettlement assistance to thousands of refugees in camps and in flight. We offer the same protection and assistance to thousands more in refugee-like situations.
Our role in selecting refugees abroad is an extremely important one that is perhaps too easily forgotten. For example, there are upwards of 1 5 million refugees in camps throughout the world. Selecting refugees from these camps is part of an obligation we have undertaken to relieve the burden on countries of first asylum, countries which are struggling to meet the needs of their own people. Very often these refugees have spent years in camps and have no hope of returning to their own countries or of being resettled locally. They are offered resettlement in Canada. It is agreed throughout the international community that although initially a refugee's most pressing need is safe haven, the ideal long-term solution is repatriation or local integration. Third country settlement away from a familiar culture, language, or landscape is the final, least preferred option. Resettlement is for the refugee who has no other choice.
Last year, and this year, the Government will sponsor and resettle 12,000 convention refugees who have applied at our embassies overseas, and who have been taken from camps. Some are interviewed in and brought out of jails, some are rescued at sea. There are also thousands of refugees brought here by groups or organizations acting as private sponsors.
The private sponsorship program has been operating since 1978. It allows all Canadians to become involved over and above what the Government is able to do. In fact, there is no limit on the number of refugees that can be brought into Canada in this manner. While the 1987 report on immigration levels estimates that there will be 5,000 privately sponsored refugees, this is not a ceiling. Many more could be admitted if the situation demanded it, and if Canadians were able to respond in kind. This becomes evident when we look at Canada's response to the Indo-Chinese boat people crisis in 1979 and 1980. The co-operation of private citizens and the federal Government saw Canada open its doors to some 60,000 Indo-Chinese refugees.
Our refugee selection program is so generous that we extend our protection to many who, strictly speaking, are not convention refugees, but who are in situations to which we feel we should respond. This is done in two ways; through the selection of people from designated countries that are undergoing strife or upheaval, and through the selection of those who warrant special humanitarian consideration.
Both of these programs offer protection to the Indo-Chinese and Eastern Europeans through resettlement. They also supplement our other refugee selection programs and assist
August 17, 1987

political prisoners, oppressed persons, self-exiles, and victims of disasters throughout the world. This year our humanitarian measures program allows up to 8,000 people to be admitted. That is over and above the 12,000 government sponsored refugees, those in the designated classes, and those privately sponsored.
We must remember that, to a large extent, it is through our overseas program that we best serve the world refugee problem. At the same time as continuing to express our commitment to refugees, we must balance our response to international developments, large-scale population movements, our international obligations, and the principles of fairness and justice. To this end Canada is working hard in many international forums to help alleviate the political, economic, and social problems which beset so many refugee producing countries.
We also work hard and in close co-operation with dozens of non-governmental organizations across the country to see that government and privately sponsored refugees, and many new immigrants as well, settle as smoothly as possible into Canadian society. I am happy to say that together we have achieved much in this area. We will continue to move ahead.
A great part of our commitment is translated into programs to ensure successful integration. Some of them start even before many refugees arrive in Canada. For instance, the revolving transportation loans fund of S90 million is used to cover transportation costs for eligible immigrants and refugees. We would like to note that loans to convention refugees and designated class applicants are interest free.
Once in Canada many refugees need our help to get their new life off to a solid start. If this is the case, the Adjustment Assistance Program helps ensure that these government sponsored newcomers have enough income to meet their basic needs. Funds available for this program total $49 million for the fiscal year 1987-88.
I would now like to mention several programs which provide ample proof of the positive and very flexible nature of the cooperation between the federal Government and NGOs. I am sure every Member of the Flouse would agree that this close co-operation can be held up as a model of its kind.
The Immigrant Settlement and Adaption Program has been developed to aid immigrant and refugee aid organizations in providing a wide range of services to the community. Through contracts with the federal Government, these activities include reception and referral services, interpretation, counselling, orientation, and general information.
This partnership has produced a nation-wide network of groups that ensure that newcomers, unfamiliar with certain facets of Canadian life, do not fall through the cracks and, may I add, they do their jobs in a highly competitive and professional manner. Funding for ISAP has grown 60 per cent
Immigration Act, 1976
in the past 2.5 years, and this fiscal year it totals almost $5 million.
As well we have set up programs such as the Host Refugee Program which is carried out jointly with community groups. Through it, government sponsored refugees have access to another source of information and, more importantly, support. Starting with an initial three pilot projects in 1985, host projects have sprung up across Canada, providing an additional safety net for those needing special attention which may not have been available before.
Briefly, then, these are the major pillars of our settlement program. We will continue to innovate, to develop, and to mould our programs as the need evolves. We are committed, as the House well knows, to reaching out to refugees in real need, to rescuing those fleeing persecution, and to responding to crises as they occur.
The more than 25,000 people coming to Canada under our humanitarian programs this year are living witnesses to an ideal which Canada will never and can never abandon. However, as the Minister of Employment and Immigration has stated time and time again, the existing system was never designed to deal with the growing number of claims or with the large number of false claims to refugee status. It is bogged down and can no longer respond effectively to genuine refugees in need of Canada's protection.
As the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) stated during a recent foray, as reported in The Globe and Mail, "the length of the process acts as a magnet for those who are not convention refugees".
The long-term solution as embroiled in Bill C-55 will give us the tools to deal with the circumstances which Canada faces now and in the future. However, we have to make changes to the existing legislation to enable us to mobilize our resources immediately and until Bill C-55 comes into place.
Clearly the deterrent and detention legislation holds the immediate answers. Bill C-84 is based on the principle of justice while achieving the balance of speed and due process which will make for a fair yet effective refugee determination process.
With the Bill and with the will of the House we have the means to act immediately, to put a halt to the most flagrant abuses of our refugee policies, and to make a start at putting our affairs in order so that we may resume our role as a champion for justice and a protector of the persecuted.
In conclusion, I want to emphasize that our domestic refugee determination system is only one of several programs and initiatives which we undertake on behalf of refugees. It is only one aspect of a much larger and wider spread commitment to refugees which is and will continue to be enshrined in our legislation.
Through the rapid passage of Bill C-84, we will be taking the steps necessary to put an immediate end to the flagrant

August 17, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
abuses of our laws and to the obstruction of our refugee program, an obstruction that keeps those truly in need from the protection they deserve.
In so doing we will send a strong message to our constituents and to the world that Canada is a country which cares about human dignity, about human safety, and about doing whatever is within our power to prevent exploitation and to ensure protection from persecution. We will also be saying that Canada is a sovereign nation; that we will protect our borders, our humanitarian values and traditions as embodied in our immigration and refugee systems; and that we will safeguard the security of our country.
Let us work together, pass Bill C-55, and therefore take the course of action needed to serve our refugee determination over the long term. Let us also consider the deterrent and detention legislation which is before us. Let us pass both Bills without delay so that the Government may deal immediately and decisively with the events at hand.

Madam Speaker, it is with a sense of dismay and almost shame that I find myself having to address in the Canadian House of Commons a piece of legislation which runs so directly counter to and which so subverts the record of humanitarian concern, caring and openness with which this country has been associated in the past.
One of the events in my life I recall most clearly is flying from England to East Africa in 1972 and stopping at the Cairo airport. I am not certain how many Hon. Members are aware of what the Cairo airport is like. It is not exactly a haven of peace. It is a hodge-podge of tremendous uncertainty and turbulence. In short, it is not a very pleasant place to be in in the middle of the night. Yet, because of transportation schedules, we had to stop there for at least three or four hours.
In the area in which we were waiting out this difficult period there was a throng of perhaps 150 or 200 Ugandan Asians. They were sitting there with looks on their faces which I can only describe as reflecting the deepest possible relief anyone could conceive of. These people had faced the all too real possibility of death or brutal torture at the hands of soldiers of the Amin regime. Yet they had been accepted by Canada as refugees. A new life for them was now possible. They had to leave behind friends and virtually all of their possessions, but they were escaping that regime and finding refuge in Canada. That is what our refugee policy has been about in the past. Our policy has been to accept thousands of Czech refugees in 1968, thousands of Hungarian refugees in 1956, and tens of thousands of Vietnamese boat people. All those people faced brutal conditions had they stayed at home, so they escaped and ultimately came to Canada.
It is possible that we could think of all this as simple humanitarianism on the part of Canada. We have been good-hearted in the past, but things have changed under the Conservative Government. Let me suggest, however, that there is a different perspective which needs to be understood. 1 venture to suggest that virtually every Member of Parliament who has canvassed his or her constituency has been struck by this, especially if that constituency is in one of the metropolitan areas of this country. If those Members are like me, they have seen these refugees become the most constructive, productive and caring citizens we could possibly have hoped for. We are not talking about some kind of good-hearted gesture of charity alone, although that should be enough. We are talking about the fact that people who have come to our

August 17, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
country as refugees have made tremendous economic contributions to Canada.
In the City of Ottawa, which took in many of the Vietnamese boat people, we can ask ourselves, how many of them are a drag on our social system? How many do you find on welfare? How many do you find living off community resources instead of contributing? The answer is, very, very few.
Speaking as an economist, I have to say that most immigrants, particularly those who have come here as refugees, have made tremendous contributions which are illustrated by some very real facts. One such fact is that immigrants have significantly lower levels of unemployment than natural-born Canadians. Another fact is that the general level of income for immigrants is higher than that of those who were born here. After all, these people had to make a tremendous effort with great courage in order to get themselves and their families here. It is not surprising to see them making a tremendous contribution.
In my own constituency I have immigrants from virtually every part of the world. Some have come here as refugees, some as ordinary immigrants. Their economic contribution alone has been tremendous. Yet we seem to have lost sight of that in this Draconian, indeed vicious legislation which the Government has brought forward.
It is not just I and my Party who talk about the viciousness of this legislation. This is something on which there is unanimity among the churches of the country, something which is surely a rare phenomenon. I can quote to you some of the material which has been sent by those church groups. For instance, a telex was sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) from virtually every church in this country; the Anglican Church, the Baptist Federation, the Canadian Council of Churches, the Council of Christian Reform Churches in Canada, the Mennonite Central Committee, the Presbyterian Church of Canada, the Religious Society of Friends, the Salvation Army, the United Church of Canada, the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, and the Canadian Religious Conference of Ontario.
In this telex, dealing specifically with this piece of legislation, they plead for a refugee determination procedure that is fair as well as fast. They urge the Prime Minister and the Government to replace Bill C-55 with different legislation which provides "access for all claimants to a full, fair and independent hearing" and to "a meaningful appeal".
That is why we suggest that this Bill should be hoisted for six months. We think that surely in the next period of time men and women of good will, many of whom are on the government benches, will see to it that new legislation is brought before the House of Commons which provides not the kind of viciousness, the kind of arbitrary constructs which exist in this piece of legislation, but instead provide that fast and
fair appeal system which people across the country are absolutely convinced is essential.
There have been various suggestions about what our constituents think. I believe that right across the country, in my constituency as well as in every other constituency of Canada, there is above all a commitment to fairness. Fairness cannot survive the arbitrary system which will meet potential refugees under this particular Bill, an arbitrary system which gives them no independent access to their own counsel, no capacity to prepare a case and no capacity to appeal if they fall into one of number of categories which leaves them outside of the restricted and privileged few which Canada will accept in the future.
That, Madam Speaker, is not the kind of country that I want Canada to become. We cannot permit that kind of arbitrary, controlled, almost fascist sort of approach to hold sway in this country. If we do permit it to start, its impact will be insidious. Its impact will grow. We will become used to this kind of arbitrariness with respect to not only people arriving as potential immigrants but with respect to how Canadians themselves are treated. That is the danger as we head down this path.
That is why I hope that the Government itself will see fit to withdraw this piece of legislation, to vote in favour of the Liberal amendment which gives it a six-month hoist, and to bring back, not nothing, not the existing system, but the very sensible, very straightforward, quite fair and quite open system which has been recommended by church groups, which has been recommended by Rabbi Plaut in his detailed study of this question, which has been recommended again and again by individuals who have studied this issue with some care.
Finally, Madam Speaker, I find it especially ironic that the Government has called back the House of Commons to deal with 174 new arrivals on the East Coast of Canada, 174 arrivals in the context of a Government that has not even been able to meet its own targets for immigration in the past year. Its own targets for immigration in 1986 were from 105,000 to 115,000 and it could not even hit 100,000.
It is not as though we are talking about a great inundation of people from outside of Canada. We are talking about what used to be a tremendous humanitarian tradition in this country. We are talking about, I hope, a tremendous humanitarian future which can only be achieved if the Government starts to listen-if it starts to listen to church groups, those who have studied the legislation in detail, those who have worked as lawyers with refugee groups, and opposition Parties in the House of Commons.
I hope that the Government will listen. It has listened in the past. I do not think it is too late for it to start now. However, I believe that for the sake of the country it is important that the listening begin very soon.

Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the comments of the Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. August 17, 1987

Langdon). 1 have served on committee with that Member in the past and he has had some very good observations to make from time to time. However, his representations today leave me very puzzled.
At the outset 1 would like to make a comment on his general remarks on refugees. There was an inference in his comments that Members on this side of the House are opposed to refugees. I deny that completely and absolutely. This country was largely built by refugees over many decades, whether economic refugees from the potato famine of Ireland, refugees from the pogroms of central Europe, the boat people, refugees from Europe after World War II, or from the uprisings in Czechoslovakia or Hungary. Those people came to Canada and were welcomed. 1 am not aware of one Member on this side of the House who in any way is opposed to refugees coming to Canada. It is a part of our country and our tradition. I invite the Member to withdraw the implication that we on this side of the House were opposed because it is totally without foundation.
My second observation concerns meaningful debate on what to do with the refugees who are coming to our shores at this time. We are supposed to be debating a six month hoist this afternoon. Members opposite do not have any kind of sinecure or lock on fairness. We are as anxious to see a fair and responsible immigration policy put in place. But it is quite obvious at this juncture that the immigration policy that is being administered is not fair because queue jumpers are able to come into this country and clog the system to the point where respect for our whole immigration policy is put in jeopardy.
We are attempting, through this special recall of Parliament, to deal meaningfully with how to evolve a fair, enforceable, reasonable and practical solution. Members opposite do not seem to be interested in that. I invite the Hon. Member to explain how he expects to get fairness if he is not prepared to discuss the issue.

Mr. Speaker, frankly, I believe that government Members live in a dream world in which somehow their ears are closed to informed opinion with respect to an issue like this.
Rabbi Gunther Plaut, a person who has studied this issue in tremendous detail, says that we are trying perhaps to build a Berlin wall, and that instead of trying to tailor refugee procedures to control abusers we ought properly to concentrate on refugees and make the procedure fair and quick.
Amnesty International, which is hardly a partisan body, calls on the Government to withdraw the Bill. It calls the Bill regrettable and says that it blocks universal access to refugees. These opinions tell me that in fact this Bill has precisely those effects. It reduces significantly the capacity of refugees to seek a fair hearing in this country. They should not come to this
Immigration Act, 1976
country and automatically get in, but should get a fair hearing. That is what is so vicious and arbitrary about this Bill.
As 1 suggested in my speech, there is an alternative. That is why I suggested that doing away with the present Bill for six months would serve the country very well.
The Council of Churches, drawing on the work of people like Gunther Plaut, has come up with what it sees as a five-stage process which would be much faster than the present system for determining refugees, at least as fast as the process will be in this legislation for those small number of refugees who get past the gate posts. If we take their advice and pursue this five-stage process, it makes it possible to do something which is fair in terms of quickness, because people cannot be left waiting as the previous legislation has done. It also would provide fairness in the sense of giving people the right to be free of arbitrary control and allowing them to make their case appropriately and have it judged and appealed with the fairness to which this country has become accustomed.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for my colleague. I want to refer to a letter from an ordinary citizen in Winnipeg. Mrs. Anna Rondinella writes about the fact that the Government has brought in legislation to amend the refugee determination process. While she is in favour of action in that area, she also points out that it is not enough to amend the refugee determination process. She would like to see at the same time an amendment to the definition of family unification so that brothers and sisters are classed as close family and qualify for family unification, especially for a person like herself who has no other family and would like to bring at least one member of her family here.
She goes on to make an appeal to the Government to be more generous in the area of family unification. She says that it is not enough for the Government to appeal to immigrant communities by trying to say that it is not fair for people to sneak in under the refugee determination process, but that it is necessary for the Government to make some changes in policies that affect family reunification. Does my colleague agree with her request that the family reunification policy be more generous so that immigrants in this country can bring their family members here, rather than have the Government simply bash refugees?

Madam Speaker, there is an emergency with respect to immigrants in this country. That emergency has hit each of us who has dealt with constituency cases over the life of this Parliament. However, that emergency has nothing to do with refugees. It is that the Government has failed to move despite many recommendations to make it easier for people to come to this country to join their families. 1 found incredible slowness in the number of cases I have personally taken forward in an attempt to get action. It is like something out of Kafka, dealing with a bureaucracy that believes that 12 months is a short time. It is ridiculous.

Madam Speaker, the question we are dealing with today is complex. We are not talking about ideas or abstract concepts but about human lives.
Bill C-55 has to do with the critical situation of those who need Canada's protection. It so happens that the measure takes into account our own Canadian standards with respect to refugee protection.
Statistics on the number of homeless refugees throughout the world are practically endless, but statistics are little more than mere figures. A refugee is a human being whose life may be endangered. Madam Speaker, it is imperative that we keep this fact in mind. Canadians are fully aware of the human aspect of this problem. A recent poll indicates that three out of four Canadians feel that people fleeing from persecution must be protected.
Still the Government is convinced that it is becoming ever more important to keep Canadians fully informed with respect to refugees and matters related to immigration. This is particularly true if Canada is to play an adequate role on the international scene with a view to finding solutions to the refugee situation.
This is why I should like to comment on the need to keep people well informed and fully aware of what is happening. This approach can only stem from a long-term vision of Canadian programs concerning immigration and refugees.
This Government has already developed a longer term vision which looks upon these programs as means to reinforce national unity and contribute to a greater economic prosperity, while meeting its humanitarian objectives.
Following the 1984, fall election, the Government reviewed its immigration policy together with the provinces, some nongovernmental organizations, university professors and other interested parties. Following this review, it came to the conclusion that it was desirable to increase the immigration levels in a moderate and controlled fashion. This increase was made to the benefit of refugees who were languishing in camps abroad.
The Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration has had the opportunity to express its views on the issue. Other countries have reduced the number of refugees they will accept. Canada, for one, has kept its doors wide open and has established no ceiling as to the number of refugees it will help resettle. Moreover, this year we are contemplating
accepting 12,000 refugees sponsored by the Government, and at least 5,000 more sponsored by private organizations and groups.
What exactly is a refugee? No public information and awareness program could follow its course without an answer to this basic question. Canada accepts the definition of refugee as established by the United Nations Convention. In short, a refugee is a person who happens to be outside his country and unable to return to it because he has a well-founded fear of being persecuted for reasons of race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership of a particular social group.
Our vision of the increasing importance of immigration for the future development of Canada is based on a series of factors. First, the economic factor: Immigrants create more jobs than they remove from the Canadian economy. They support economic growth and development by contributing to capital formation, increasing the demand for Canadian goods and services, bringing to the labour market their drive and much sought after expertise, and contributing to the tax revenues of all levels of Government. Socially, immigrants contribute to the ongoing development and diversification of the Canadian multicultural mosaic by which all our Canadian regions are socially and culturally enriched. That 70 per cent of immigrants belong to the category of family members underlines the emphasis given by Canada to the reunification of families by welcoming members who had remained abroad.
As far as demography is concerned, increased immigration levels will enable us to prevent the decline in the Canadian population projected for the end of the 20th century and the beginning of the 21st century. There are a number of misconceptions that will be dispelled by informing the people. For instance, some people believe that when refugees arrive they steal the place away from legitimate immigrants. That is not the case, Madam Speaker. As Carol Goar pointed out in the Toronto Star, "This is tantamount to suggesting that people coming to hospital emergency take the places of people waiting for elective surgery".
Our action in support of refugees from across the world has been recognized by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, who awarded the Nansen Medal to the Canadian people. Further, Canada plays an important role in permanent discussions of the High Commission for Refugees and OECD on how to implement the broad international action approaches to the regulation of the movement of some 70 to 80 million migrants in the world.
As I said earlier, Madam Speaker, our doors remain open to refugees. I would like to point out that they also remain open to immigrants.
The 1987 level planning range is 115,000 to 125,000, much more than the low level to which the Liberal Government had let the movement decline. The Government recently held consultations with provinces, non-government organizations
August 17, 1987

universities and other parties on the direction to be given to the Immigration Program for the rest of the decade. It is evident from these consultations that we will likely need higher levels of immigration over the next decade to meet our own needs and to honour our international obligations. Departments concerned are presently evaluating the social and economic impacts of immigration on Canada while projected immigration levels for the 1990's are being established.
Madam Speaker, the Government of which I am a part is convinced that immigration represents an important factor in the economic and social well-being of Canada, one which has allowed us to take a leadership role in finding solutions at the international level to the problem of refugees and immigrants seeking assistance on humanitarian grounds.
It has taken some time to elaborate a long term perspective and this is partly due to the narrow view of the future which characterized the undertakings of the former liberal administration. We are now focussing on more effective means to make Canadians aware of the facts about immigration and the advantages which can result. In this regard of course, we give special consideration to the noteworthy efforts of nongovernmental organizations and to their information and public awareness programs.
Our consultation process with regard to immigration levels is among the most open and detailed in the world. It provides a better understanding of the impact of issues which have a bearing on immigration and refugees.
At the present time, Madam Speaker, the Government is carrying out consultations on immigration levels with nongovernmental organizations which involve 150 national organizations, 500 regional organizations and 40 university organizations, as well as with representatives of the provinces and the territories. During the last series of national and regional consultations we had no less than 23 meetings on administrative matters pertaining to immigration levels for 1988, 1989 and 1990.
Recently, in Toronto, we had a two-day meeting with national ethnocultural organizations to discuss questions concerning immigration and refugees. That meeting, the first since the beginning of the 1980s, reflects the Government commitment to a greater involvement of ethnic communities in the determination of immigration levels.
A thorough consultation process is the first element of an effective information program on immigration matters. The Employment and Immigration Commission has produced a series of free consultation reports on our programs and policies. At a time when we are almost always trying to recover costs, Employment and Immigration Canada continues to make documents available free of charge, to promote exchange of information. These documents are in addition to a wide range of free booklets already available.
Immigration Act, 1976
Passage of Bill C-55 will naturally require that new documents be prepared to inform claimants, counsels, parliamentarians and the general public of the new process. An important element of a well-conceived information program is a research program to make the population aware of some of the key policies and issues actively discussed regarding the immigration program.
Employment and Immigration Canada has undertaken to prepare a series of research documents to that end. Up to now we have published free booklets on aging of the population and immigration and on the impact of immigration on employment. Others to be published will deal with immigration of children and the relationship betweem immigration and migration.
In addition to these studies, Employment and Immigration Canada has a program of technical research in various areas, such as the settlement of immigrants and refugees, immigration and the economy, control policies and operations.
Two advisory committees made up of academics were created last spring to contribute to communications, research and initiatives. One will examine demographic factors, and the other the social and economic aspects of immigration.
Madam Speaker, to develop an extended information program, there have to be extensive consultations and detailed research. Employment and Immigration Canada is now looking at ways to publicize this program in Canada. The methods now being used or considered include the following:
Creating posters and information modules on immigration and demographic evolutions;
Organizing workshops on immigration for certain key groups, such as Members of Parliament, media representatives and teachers;
Writing articles to explain the new policy and program changes;
And I could quote many others.
Other initiatives to improve information on this program will be undertaken before the end of this year. The Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) has recently underlined the high priority which will be given to such initiatives. I am convinced that we can count on the support of our honourable collegues in this regard.
An information program naturally requires an exchange between the one who gives and the one who receives the message. These last few months, Canadians have become aware of the difficult decision which must be made in relation with immigration and refugee programs. The Government now intends to emphasize the major contribution of immigrants on the social, humanitarian, economic and demographic levels.
Before closing, I would like to go over certain facts about Bill C-55.

August 17, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
Last Tuesday, August 11, Canadians were told once again and more firmly about the clear intention of the Government to implement quickly mechanisms to counter abuses related with the refugee determination process and to enable the Government to protect bona fide refugees.
The measures which the Government is planning to take are aimed at those people who show up at our borders or airports without papers or with false documents, as well as the smugglers who, through their fraudulent actions, are helping the entry into Canada of illegal aliens.
Under Bill C-55, the carriers will have to make sure that the people they are bringing to Canada are duly in possession of the required documents, failing which they could be liable to a heavy fine or a long prison term.
The Government is determined to have this Bill adopted. The Canadian public will have to strike a just balance between the need for compassion and understanding on the one hand and irresponsibility on the other. If we do not stop soon the abuse of our refugee status determination process, Canada's reputation as a country with integrity will be jeopardized. We will become the laughing-stock of a great many nations.
The Government is determined to defend its borders, but it will not allow regrettable incidents to become deplorable precedents and have its reputation as a country which accepts true refugees tarnished.
Many people have come forward to explain the Government's intentions. These intentions should not be questioned. I therefore ask all Hon. Members to remove all obstacles and finally put an end to a sorry state of affairs which we should not tolerate any longer.
Canadians will be able to share the Government's vision about its immigration policy and will be able to better support and understand its objectives concerning immigration and refugees.
Madam Speaker, many polls have been carried out. I was puzzled by one of them which was carried out throughout Canada and where the following question was asked: Do you agree that people jumping the line, those who are coming illegally into Canada should have the same protections under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms as all other Canadians?
And surprisingly, and this is for my friends in the New Democratic Party, 80 per cent of those who say they would support a NDP Government are responding: No, we do not agree.
I will say to my dear friends in the New Democratic Party what it means:	it means that your members, your
"supporters", are people who agree with the efforts made by this Government to try to protect real refugees who are coming into Canada, but also to put in place a legislation that will allow us to "give the boot", as your leader, Mr. Ed Broadbent, said so eloquently on February 1 1, 1987, to give them the boot if we find that they are not bona fide refugees. He was answering a question put by Mr. Webster during a BCTV
program. Therefore, if the NDP Leader agrees with our position, why do members of the New Democratic Party, under the leadership of Mr. Broadbent, not agree with Bill C-55 which is supported by all Canadians?

Madam Speaker, 1 am puzzled by the speech made by the Hon. Member for Portneuf (Mr. Ferland) who just completed his remarks. On the one hand he tells us that the Government and the Department of Employment and Immigration are holding lengthy, detailed and careful consultations with people from one end of the country to the other on what should be our policy with regard to immigration and refugees. On the other hand, while supposedly holding these consultations, the Government brought in two Bills. It brought in those Bills before it could hear from the people with whom the Hon. Member says the Government is consulting. I find that hard to understand and 1 would like the Hon. Member to explain.
I would also like the Hon. Member to explain why the Bills we have contain so few of the recommendations made by the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration which held a large number of meetings and which made a unanimous report. This committee is a committee on which a majority of members, because of the composition of the House, are members of the Conservative Party.
Why does the Hon. Member urge us to ignore the opposition expressed to these two Bills by, among other organizations, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, which represents almost all of the new immigrant groups which have come to Canada in recent years, the Canadian Jewish Congress, the Canadian Labour Congress, Amnesty International, and virtually every one of the major churches in the country? All of these groups have expressed their very strong opposition to the major provisions of these two Bills while accepting the idea that we need to have a system which is humane, fair and which does not allow people to jump to the head of the line in front of many who have waited for years to have their applications dealt with.

Madam Speaker, I said that Employment and Immigration Canada had indeed consulted the Canadian people since last spring.
But for the New Democrats, consultation is forever. When you consult people, it does not take 14 months to know what they think about a bill. We do not need to talk things over. But I think that for New Democrats, it has become a tradition. They like talking, but they do not react or act very often. They would rather have lots of people lose their time. We went through a consultation process. It is going on and will continue in the future. The Bill before us is a result of that consultation.
August 17, 1987

You said that certain agencies were opposed to the measures advocated in Bill C-55. You must remember as well that last February if my memory serves me right-indeed this position was supported by some journalists-people were saying that the temporary measures which we as the Government had taken were unacceptable. It was impossible,
But I see today that Mr. Vennat in La Presse is suggesting that we ought to use those methods. They are good methods now, but were not so at that time.
Apparently the Opposition is reacting much in the same way today. In February we were using harsh methods, but today we ought to get back to the methods used in February and say they are the best available. The ones we advocate in Bill C-55 are no good.
I have yet to see a measure tabled by this Government in the House have the good fortune of being agreeable for even a fraction of a second to the Opposition. Madam Speaker, instead of suggesting ways to improve this Bill, the Opposition is engaged in outright boycott. They are saying: The Bill is no good. They fail to propose anything better.
That's not true.
You have been saying that for months and years on end, but I have yet to see any results. And you don't seem to listen very often to your constituents. If you listened more often . . .

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. much as two years to accept the recommendations of this Standing Committee, instead of taking action and putting together a system which would ensure a more rapid treatment of these applications, a more efficient administration to ensure that the waiting list of some 20,000 refugees would not be as long as now.

Madam Speaker, at issue is not whether one is for or against measures to punish the smugglers of false refugees. The New Democratic Party answers yes. At issue is the way to do it. Madam Speaker, I should like to call my hon. friend's attention to an information document. I see that when the time comes for them to obtain information, the NDP people are not in a hurry. It is my belief that Canadians are aware of those facts and appreciate that we must do something about it. When Canadians read, as hopefully the Hon.
