speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The period for questions and comments after the speech of the Hon. Member for Portneuf (Mr. Ferland) is now ended. So is the first eight-hour period of debate. Accordingly, speeches will now last 10 minutes. Debate. I recognize the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone).

August 17, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976

Madam Speaker, I followed with interest the contribution made by the Hon. Member for Portneuf (Mr. Ferland) and I feel that once again he emphasizes that Canada has an open door for immigrants and used to have an open door for refugees. Unfortunately, such is not the direction that has now been chosen by the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard). This is a sham, and they are playing all kinds of tricks to keep confusing Canadians as to who is a legitimate refugee and who is an immigrant. I believe that as Minister of State for Immigration and Minister of Employment and Immigration, their job is to uphold the place of immigrants and the role they can play, and that refugees who become immigrants are welcome here. This is what they forgot to do and everyone is confused.
The lack of support for both the immigrant and the increase in family rejoining has become an unpleasant and unnecessary game plan on the part of the Minister of State for Immigration, and the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Instead of being clear, candid, and forthright and explaining that we are discussing two separate streams, there has been an incredible tendency to make the population in general feel that a person who is coming in as a bogus refugee is displacing the person who is an immigrant. That is false. The Government has gone to great length not to explain this to the general population.
There is a desire and need to improve the family reunification clauses that are in the present Immigration Act. The Equality for All report deposited in the House almost two years ago called for those changes, but nothing has happened. Now we see a refugee Bill that is restrictive. It has caused the United Nations people to request that we stop the type of abuse we are thinking of.
There is something wrong when traditionally Canadians have such a proud record. We were awarded the Nansen Medal for what we have done. We have brought into this country people who have enriched the tissue, the fabric, the expression, and quality of life for all Canadians from the economic and the social perspectives. Representatives from Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Uganda, Cyprus, Vietnam, Poland, Iran, El Salvador, Lebanon, Sri Lanka, and Guatemala live within the constituency of Mount Royal. I have spoken with them. In this regard, these people are not pleased with the performance of the Conservative Government. They are being made to feel uncomfortable as immigrants, as if they were asking for special favours because they want to have what is an extended family and their basic family considered. All they have received is words but no action.
Where there are refugees awaiting a determination of their status, from the Tamils all the way through to the people of
the Caribbean Islands, et cetera, they are being destabilized, they are uncomfortable, and they have a sense of dislocation. Is it not enough that they have had to suffer the trauma of dislocation? If Hon. Members opposite think they can say, "Wait, I am going to run back for my American Express card, my papers, and my visa", when their lives are being threatened and when they are in danger, believe me, that is not what refugees do. They are refugees because they feel threatened and they are no longer able to live their lives in peace and harmony. Their surroundings are no longer places of peace and harmony or places where they can live properly.
We have the unhappy situation of uprooting and the trauma of dislocation for refugees, and we are saying to these same people, "Refugees, go home". Most of them would go home; if they felt they could, they would. This is what we tend to forget.
I should like to suggest that the Minister of State for Immigration ought to read from Isaiah and then translate it into French for the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard). I suggest that he recall the following:
Woe to you! you who make unjust laws and publish burdensome decrees,
depriving the poor of justice, robbing the weakest of my people of their rights.
International human rights indicate that Canada is a land of refuge for those in need. Your very Draconian, unfair, and inhuman approach to both immigrant streams-you promise but you do not deliver-and refugees whom you treat with disgrace will come to haunt each and every one of you, believe me.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May 1 remind the Hon. Member that she should address her remarks through the Chair. The same rule applies on both sides of the House.

Madam Speaker, I thank you for that reminder. I suggest that there is a serious and real problem. That was addressed by the Robinson report, the Plaut report, and the standing committee report. How many more reports should there be? Maybe they should go back to school and learn to read; then they could follow these reports.
All those reports are in. They have had the suggestions and recommendations which they have totally ignored. They have followed their own little sweet path. I do not know who dreamt up the lines.
Perhaps it is better that they bring in the hoist, go out and talk to the constituency, hear what the NGOs, the churches and the synagogues have to say, and hear what the people who wrote the reports have to say. Did Rabbi Plaut find the response reasonable? Did he find that response acceptable? They can be assured that he did not.
What did Tom Clark, a worker for the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees, have to say? He said:
Instead of access there is a screen, instead of bringing Canada a notch ahead
of European countries, the immigration minister has brought it down to their
level. It's despicable.
August 17, 1987

What did Michael Schelew of Amnesty International have to say? He said:
It's an about-face on Canada's humanitarian record, that may place people
fleeing persecution in jeopardy.
Who is listening in the Conservative Party, for goodness' sake? Is it not about time that you listened to the population who elected you?
We are.

Excuse me, Madam Speaker. 1 think government Members should take heed of what is being said.
A rather well known personality internationally, Elie Wiezel, winner of the Nobel Prize, said:
! believe that a society can be measured and judged by its attitude towards
strangers ... 1 would hope that Canada would like to be measured according
to these lofty rules. I say Canada should lead by example.
I do not think Canada's example should be how to pick a safe third country, how to have two people at the border determining one's future, how not to have access to the legal process, or how not to do anything in the best interest of helping a person who is in crying need to get to safe waters.
The weaknesses of Bill C-55 are many. They are opposed by the NGOs. Its shortcomings include the prescreening system, the safe third country concept, the refugee determination board, to which no one can get because it is surrounded by all kinds of blockages, the appeal system, and the precedent which Canada has set for other countries by perhaps encouraging them to consider similar action. Certainly turning a blind eye to the refugees of the world is one thing Canadians need not do in a country of wealth and space which can use good, healthy, determined people who are looking to start a new life, much as it is uncomfortable, and to run away from the place they knew as home.
Canada is large. It is wealthy. It is rich in human and material resources, but it is not without its blemishes.
I only hoped that all of us in the Chamber learned from our blemishes-the indigenous people of Canada and those who fled Nazi persecution. 1 have not forgotten the story of the St. Louis at the Port of Montreal or the shores of Canada where refugees went back and then went through extermination camps. If one person has to do that, I hope the Ministers and that caucus will give serious thought to why their consciences will not let them sleep.
We were not kind and considerate to Canadians of Japanese origin. We have done many things which have been wrong. However, I think over time we have become a more humane society and a more concerned society with a better appreciation of the multitude of cultures, languages, skin colours, and faces of people who have come to enrich the tapestry that is Canada today.
Let us not be narrow-minded and bigoted or respond to the basest of feelings expressed out there. Let us be sure that we give a fair hearing to the refugees who come to our shores.
Immigration Act, 1976

Madam Speaker, the City of Winnipeg which I represent, for 100 years or more has been the gateway to western Canada for people coming to this country.
My own constituency, with the exception of several thousands of native people who live in it, consists of people who are themselves immigrants or whose parents or grandparents came to Canada as did my father some 80 years ago. The original immigrants who settled in my area came from Great Britain, Ukraine, Poland, Germany, and other eastern European countries. We have had an influx since World World II of people from Portugal, the Philippines, Italy, China, Hong Kong, Vietnam, Laos, Central American countries such as Nicaragua and El Salvador, and Caribbean countries such as Jamaica and Trinidad.
They are very interested in the kinds of policies which Canada adopts and implements with respect to immigrants who wish to come to this country and with respect to refugees.
More than half the people who come to see me when I am in my office have problems related to immigration. They are people who want to help members of their families, living in the countries from which they came, and come to Canada. Our rules and definition of who can be considered family are so restrictive that in nearly every case I must tell them that I am sorry but their relatives do not qualify for entry to Canada.
We are dealing with two Bills respecting immigration and refugees. They have been drafted in such a way as to make one believe that the Government has almost deliberately set out to ignore the recommendations made by a number of studies commissioned by the Government, or by the unanimous recommendations made by the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration.
I think Hon. Members should note the speech made in the House several days ago by the Chairman of that committee and his criticism of the legislation that the Government brought forward.
The fact is that virtually every organization interested in these questions has expressed opposition to the provisions of these two Bills. I should like to name a few-the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, the Canadian Jewish Congress, the Canadian Labour Congress, and Amnesty International. Thirteen of the largest church organizations in Canada sent a telex to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on June 1 of this year in which they expressed their very strong opposition to many clauses in these two Bills. Included among these churches are the Anglican Church, the Canadian Baptist Federation, the Canadian Council of Churches, the Council of Christian Reform Churches, the Mennonite Central Committee, the Presbyterian Church, the Salvation Army, the Quakers, the United Church, the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, and the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees.

August 17, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
To indicate how strongly many people feel about this legislation, I want to tell Hon. Members that I was today in communication with people from Winnipeg and other parts of Manitoba who have worked to help facilitate the movement of refugees into Canada, representatives of the Anglican Church, the Roman Catholic Church and the Mennonite Church, and they told me that if this Bill is passed and the work they do is considered contrary to the law and they are charged, tried and sentenced, they are prepared to go to prison. They believe that the work they are doing to help refugees come to Canada is so right and so justified that they are prepared to pay the penalty they may have to face.
These are people who are not political. They are not wildeyed radicals. These are people who have a firm commitment to seeing that justice is done.
What is wrong with this Bill? First, it is inaccessible. Instead of ensuring that all those arriving in Canada claiming to be refugees can have their claims heard, this legislation seeks ways to return them to other countries. This legislation has no provision for a meaningful appeal process. The initial screening can only be appealed from out of the country. There is no requirement that a written reason be given at this stage, thus making a legal appeal difficult. The second stage oral hearing can be appealed but only to the Federal Court and only on matters of law, not fact. We know what kind of legal costs that process would entail.
There is no provision in the Bill for humanitarian or compassionate cases as there is in the present legislation. Currently, about 12 per cent of cases that do not meet the technical definition are allowed to stay in the country by compassionate people and even cabinet Ministers. That will cease when this Bill is passed.
This Bill politicizes the refugee process by putting emphasis on whether or not the applicant stopped in a safe third country. Cabinet will decide what constitutes a safe third country. Inevitably, diplomatic and political pressures will intervene. The Minister has already been reluctant to deal with the case of the United States and Salvadoran refugees.
1 want to point out that under the same kind of legislation that is being proposed here, the United States has already arrested, charged, tried and convicted church workers in Texas, Arizona and New Mexico. That is the kind of legislation this Government is proposing for Canada.
This Bill is unnecessarily harsh. Rabbi Gunther Plaut before the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration suggested that what we need is fast, efficient and fair alternatives with widespread public support. We do not have that with this Bill.
This Bill attacks true refugees rather than zeroing in on those who try to abuse the system. If the Government were to bring in proposals designed to get tough with those who are trying to get around the system, the kind of people who have organized the boat expeditions and are ripping off refugees, the kind of people who make hundreds of thousands of dollars by arranging for these boat trips, we would support the legislation. We New Democrats will not support this legislation which uses an atomic bomb to kill a mosquito.
This Bill builds a Berlin wall around the country rather than promoting the humanitarianism for which Canada has been known. Furthermore, Bill C-55 harms the prospects of Canadian citizens and landed immigrants seeking to sponsor the immigration of family members from their countries of origin by reducing their effective right to appeal decisions on sponsorship.
Like every other Hon. Member from urban Canada, I have dealt with constituents who want to help relatives come to Canada but have been told by me that it is impossible because of the rules. We cannot support legislation like that. We are prepared to support any proposal the Government might make which would give us a fair, humanitarian, efficient and quick system for deciding legitimate applications, both for refugees and immigrants. That is something we do not have in the two Bills which are before us at the present time.

Madam Speaker, the legislative process works well if the Government in power recognizes the value of the advice given it by experts in the field. If it does not recognize the value of advice given it by churches, human rights groups and opposition Members, then it produces a Bill which does not deal properly and effectively with the requirements of the situation. That is exactly what is happening in the case of Bill C-55.
Canadians who are knowledgeable about the situation recognize in this Bill some travesties which, if put into effect, will do a great deal of harm not only to the people affected directly by them, including immigrants and refugees, but also to Canada's international reputation. We proudly accepted a prize for being the country that best dealt with the refugee situation. We accepted a prize for being the most generous, for opening our doors and accepting people who were less fortunate than us. We proudly accepted that award and, in the light of that acceptance, we should put in place a Bill which continues the recognition of that generosity. We should put in place the kind of structure which allowed Canada to be generous enough to win the award.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   PARITY PRICES FOR FARM PRODUCTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, June 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Nystrom that Bill C-221, an Act respecting parity prices for farm products, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   PARITY PRICES FOR FARM PRODUCTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to make a few comments on Bill C-221. The purpose of the Bill is to provide parity prices to farmers based on a cost of production formula for wheat, oats and barley used for human consumption in Canada, and to establish voluntary marketing commissions for pork and beef.
We know the farmers of this country are having very serious problems. If it is not in one area, it is in some other area. We have heard over the last year or so the tremendous difficulties our western wheat farmers are having mainly because of world market conditions. U.S. farmers are being subsidized to the point of undercutting our farmers. EEC farmers are also heavily subsidized. We are, of course, all competing for the same markets. As well, we in this country have some very high production costs. While we are extremely productive, we do have some difficulties which are caused mainly by our geography in getting our products to market.
This Bill calls for a parity price within Canada related to the cost of production. There is no question that farmers need to have a return on their investment. That investment is immense even when compared to almost all other forms of business. Equipment and machinery is extremely expensive, not to mention the cost of land. We also have the additional problems of climatic conditions. Given that, there is no question that we in this House and in the provincial legislatures across the country should do everything we can in order to help our primary producers stay on the land and support their families and industry.
Agriculture, in one form or another, is the backbone of this country. Without it our country could not survive for very long. That is why we should be doing everything we can to help our farmers survive. In hard times we have to dig down into the coffers of Government occasionally in order to support the industry.
We are supporting not only the farmers, we are supporting every consumer. We often do not think of farmers as consumers but they are probably the greatest consumers we have. Their purchases of farm equipment and machinery create jobs, mainly in central Canada, and keep people at work. Farmers are great consumers. Not necessarily more than anyone else at the dinner table, but consumers of goods and services.
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
I only had time to go through this Bill quickly a few moments ago, but I would like to see it go to committee for further study. 1 certainly have some questions I would like to ask. For example, Clause 11 deals with establishing marketing boards. We want to make sure that the majority of farmers agree with this concept. It would be very helpful if we could bring our agricultural community, in the form of the National Farmers Union and the Federation of Agriculture and other organizations which represent that community, before the committee to see if something like this would work on a voluntary basis and whether the community would agree totally to this concept.
Of course, we now have legislation on the books, both provincial and federal, which provides for the setting up of marketing boards and commissions. In that respect I have to come back to the farmers I represent, that is, potato farmers. I know the difficulties they have had over the years. They generally say they are very fortunate if they can get one good year out of every four or five. Yet that is not good enough. There has to be a better way, not only in marketing but in bringing some stability to the industry. Last year, of course, was a reasonably good year for those farmers. We are hopeful that this year will be good, but people in my province are very worried about the low rain conditions. We will know within a few days pretty well whether we are going to have the kind of yield we normally have. Indications are right now that it will be much lower than last year because of drought conditions.
What is important is not only what you produce and how much, but what you get for it. Fishermen and farmers always seem to be faced with the great dilemma of producing a product and not knowing until after they produced it what they are going to be paid for it. Therefore, if there is anything that we can do in that respect through this Bill, I would like to see it go to committee so that we can make a determined effort to do it.
I applaud the mover of this Bill for putting it forward for discussion so that we can take a hard look at it. 1 hope something good will come out of it, not only for us as Members of Parliament but especially for our primary producers.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   PARITY PRICES FOR FARM PRODUCTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must say that I cannot in any way claim to be an expert on agricultural issues. I cannot even claim to be someone who knows this policy area in any detail. However, I do want to say as a Member of Parliament from an urban riding in the City of Winnipeg that agriculture is important to us. Even if we are not tilling the fields ourselves, agricultural policy affects our quality of life. That which the Government does to farmers is important to us. The policy framework put in place for farming communities is important to us.
As I understand it, this legislation deals with the concept of parity pricing. Like most of the people in my riding, 1 cannot tell you exactly what parity pricing is, but 1 can tell you my

August 17, 1987
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
understanding of it. I understand it to be an opportunity for a farmer to earn his bread, to make a living.
Farmers should have their costs covered when they sell their product and they should earn a fair return on their investment. That is what all Canadians expect whether they work for someone else or have a small business, or even a large corporation. They expect to be able to earn their living from the sweat of their brow, from the hard work they put into their enterprise.
I have learned from my colleagues in my caucus who come from farming constituencies that in today's economy in order for farmers to be able to make a living they must have parity pricing. In order for them to be able to cover their costs of farming they must have parity pricing. Their costs of producing must be covered and they must earn a fair return on their investment.
One renowned and noted parliamentarian, John George Diefenbaker, came from the west and spoke eloquently in this Elouse. With regard to parity pricing he said that farmers want parity, not charity. In other words, they want an opportunity to earn a living rather than having to go into bankruptcy or live on welfare or public subsidies. This legislation asks for simple economic justice. It asks that a farmer who tills his soil and runs his business be able to make a living from his efforts. I think that that is only fair.
The international agricultural wars that have been going on for the last while have made it obvious to urban dwellers that agriculture is an important issue which touches them directly. The Americans and the European Economic Community so grossly oversubsidize their farmers that they are able to grab markets which have traditionally been Canadian. They drive down the international price of grain to a level at which even those farmers who raise grain in the most productive land in the world for grain, which is western Canada, cannot compete.
The international grain war has caught a lot of attention in the media and has brought agricultural issues home to urban Canadians. It also points out the need for government action. It is not enough to be able to plant your seed in the spring and hope to harvest in the fall. The Government must put in place the appropriate public policy framework.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) has done farmers a favour by bringing forward this legislation with regard to parity pricing. In addition to putting this kind of policy in place the Government must be capable of negotiating effectively on the international scene in order to bring an end to the trade wars between the Americans and Europeans so that Canadian farmers will be able to sell their grain on the international market and earn a living.
John George Diefenbaker knew farmers well. While he was not a member of our Party, he hit the nail on the head in agricultural policy when he said that farmers want parity, not charity. In other words, they want to be able to stand on their
own two feet. They want to earn their living rather than beg for hand-outs. They do not want to have to go bankrupt.
Over the last year we have heard on an increasing basis about farmers going bankrupt. These people produce a needed product but have to sell it at such a low price that they cannot stay in business. In addition to this being unfair to farmers and their families it is a destruction of rural Canada.
Our rural communities are made up of farming families. If our farming families go into bankruptcy, there will be a devastation of rural Canadians. There will be fewer and larger corporate farms rather than the traditional family farm. As long as the present policies continue, rural communities in which people get to know one another and support one another will be a passing scene. It would be a great loss to Canada to lose our rural communities and end up with a large corporate enterprise approach to farming.
The Private Members' legislation introduced by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville which deals with parity pricing is meant to give farmers the opportunity to earn their living, to do what every Canadian considers to be his right, that is, to get up in the morning and, by the sweat of his brow, earn his income with a sense of pride in being a farmer and a Canadian. It is clear that for more and more farmers that is not possible today. The cost of producing grain and red meat is more than they can earn in the market-place. Unless we want to have a country without farms which, of course, is totally unacceptable and inconceivable, we must put in place policies which will allow farmers to cover their cost of production and earn a fair return on their investment. That, Madam Speaker, is fair.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   PARITY PRICES FOR FARM PRODUCTS ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a privilege to be able to participate in this debate which is obviously of primary concern to western farmers and to all Canadians who are committed to maintaining a farm economy and understand the role of the family farm as one of the basic building blocks in terms of our social structure, not only in western Canada but throughout the country.
Hon. Members will know that the Central Experimental Farm is in my constituency, which gives me some added basis on which I can make a contribution to this debate on Bill C-221 which was introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom).
When I read the Bill, I anticipate that if some Hon. Members from the Conservative Party were to comment on it they would express great concern that the Bill proposes a marketing commission for beef, for pork or for grain.
The fact is that this is a means by which we can legislatively create a framework by which farmers can be assured of an adequate income for their important contribution to our society. Canada has one of the most efficient agricultural sectors in the world and we have overcome many obstacles,
August 17, 1987

including a harsh climate. We also must deal with the problem of subsidization which takes place in other countries.
I suppose it is fair to say that if there were not the degree of subsidization that exists in the common market, for example, perhaps some of these measures would not be required. Nevertheless, we live in a world where national governments tend to give a certain amount of precedence to their agricultural sectors, even in countries with much less efficiency in agriculture than we have in Canada. The question is whether we simply leave our farmers in a situation where they will literally be forced into bankruptcy.
I know that in Ontario it is now difficult for a land-owner with agricultural land to rent to find anyone to rent that land for anything more than a peppercorn rent. The reason is that the land does not pay to farm.
In western Canada where the average farm size has grown to some 1,000 acres, out of necessity, the farm sector cannot be maintained by farmers renting out land to one another. The sector will have to be based on the continuation of family farms.
That raises the question of whether farmers will be able to stay in business with the present price of grains. Over the last few years the price of wheat, oats and barley has come down substantially. In today's terms, I am told, that after the cost of freight and handling, the return to a farmer on No. 3 red spring wheat is some $2 a bushel, which is down from about $4 between 1978 and 1980, which were good years. In the early 1970s the price was also about $2 a bushel in net terms. In other words, over the succeeding time when the price of goods such as clothing and other necessities for which a farmer must pay have gone up, the net return on the wheat has been about $2 per bushel. The family car that cost perhaps $6,000 in 1974, today costs some $12,000 or $14,000.
Producers have succeeded in offsetting the falling prices to some extent by increasing their yields, but that has essentially come to an end. The figures speak for themselves. In northern Saskatchewan, for example, a producer who is efficient can get up to 40 to 45 bushels per acre of yield of excellent red spring wheat. At $2 a bushel, 45 bushels gives about $90 in net return. For a farmer with 700 or 800 acres in production it means perhaps $80,000 in return, net of freight and handling but not net of the other costs. These other costs include fertilizer, diesel fuel for the tractor, and the cost of payments for equipment which may have been financed. There is the cost of the seed and all the other costs entailed in running a farm. This must be paid out of the $80,000.
There may be a mortgage on all or part of the farm, particularly if it is a young farmer who has been trying to set up, or has had to buy a farm from the parents since they do not have pensions.
Obviously, farmers have great difficulty surviving. Most farmers in the West today are literally paying to put crops in the ground in order to harvest and sell them. In other words,
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
they are poorer by putting the crop in than if they did not put any crop in at all.
Is it such a radical suggestion to say that there should be parity pricing in this particular area on domestically sold output of grains? Surely the answer is no. Presently, we have a two-price system, which I realize the Americans are trying to eliminate as part of their onslaught on Canadian practices under the free trade talks. Nevertheless, we have a two-price system now under which the price for domestically consumed grains is substantially more to the farmer than the price of grains that are sold on the world market. This Bill simply entrenches that to make sure that the farmer can count on that lasting for longer than the whim of whatever government happens to be in power.
The other part of the Bill deals with the question of establishing a voluntary system of marketing boards for red meat, for beef, and for pork. It is crazy that we have marketing boards for turnips, beets, tomatoes and almost any kind of farm product one can imagine, but not for red meats. The cost of production in the red meat producing sector is closer to what people are receiving presently, so the problem may not be so imminent. However, why can we not be expanding our sales of red meat to markets like Japan and other markets in Asia where they are beginning to consume more meats that are very expensive to produce? In the Japanese market, meat is produced locally at $25 a pound, when we could ship and land Canadian steak for $2.50 a pound. We must look into that situation.
I suggest that it is no different to guarantee a certain return to beef producers, within reason, than it is to guarantee a certain return to workers in a farm machinery plant where they have a union and organize in order to have a decent living. If workers who produce the farm equipment can have a decent living, why cannot farmers who produce the food on which we depend also enjoy a reasonable living? We are not talking about boondoggles or raising prices unreasonably as far as consumers are concerned. We are talking about a system that will provide a levelling out and ensure justice for farmers who produce the food on the one hand, ensure that those who handle and deal with produce can make a fair living and also ensure that consumers are dealt with equitably. That is the structure of this Bill.
I believe this is the last day of debate for this Bill and I urge all Members to allow it to go to a legislative committee which has been set up to consider it. Some changes may be required to the Bill when it is considered in committee, but I believe the principles are acceptable and desired by many farmers. I believe they are acceptable to many Canadian consumers as well. I hope the House will endorse the Bill at second reading today.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to join the debate today. Let me begin by congratulating the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
August 17, 1987
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
Nystrom) for bringing the Bill before the House and persuading the Standing Committee on Private Members' Business to deem this Bill worthy of coming to a vote as it meets the criteria for votable items as set by the committee.
We are at a point in this Parliament when we are voting on some of the Private Members' Bills as a result of a new procedure set up for voting on Private Members' Business. As one who was involved with that reform, I find this to be an exciting time in the life of this Parliament. I do not think that the vote with respect to parity pricing will have the same tension or controversy as the vote which took place in the House with respect to abortion, but it is an example of how matters which might not otherwise come to a vote in the House can be decided.
The House will have an opportunity to express itself on this issue and I hope it will use this opportunity to send the Bill to a committee so that it can receive the appropriate attention. That way attention will be paid indirectly to the wider issue of agriculture in Canada in the future by the legislative committee when it looks at this particular Bill.
It is important that this Bill be accepted by the House because apart from its details and apart from what may or may not work with respect to the Bill, there would be an acceptance of the notion that in a country like Canada, in the year 1987, we should no longer put farmers in the position of producing the necessities of life for less than the cost of production. It is a bizarre situation when farmers are constantly put in the position of producing what we all know needs to be produced, grains and red meats, and have to do that for less than the cost of production.
What is involved here is the principle that farmers should be guaranteed both the cost of production and the return on their labour and the investment they make when they produce those necessities. I do not understand why that should be such a controversial matter. It seems to me that almost everyone could agree with that. It is a notion which has been around for a long time.
I am mindful of what a former Prime Minister of Canada said with respect to western grain farmers: "The western Canadian farmers want parity. They do not want charity". The Right Hon. John Diefenbaker used to say that, and this afternoon in this House Members have an opportunity to put into practice that statement and give parliamentary life to that principle by sending the Bill to the appropriate committee to have it studied.
How long can farmers go on when they are constantly put in the position of having to produce the necessities of life for less than the cost of production? I do not say that just with respect to the effect it has on some individual farmers and their families. 1 say it also with respect to the broader wellbeing of Canada as a whole and of the environment. In this respect I would like to say that as the price continues to fall lower and lower, more pressure is put on individual farmers to do things
that are not in the long run in their best interests or in the best interests of Canada. I am thinking of the way in which farmers have been pressured, particularly in recent years, to put marginal land into production in order to increase their income through volume. Because the price for their produce has been so low they have attempted to meet that personal financial crisis by putting more and more land into production, thereby eliminating wildlife habitat.
A great deal of concern exists in western Canada with respect to the elimination of the habitat of waterfowl. I was pleased to see that the Manitoba Government recently entered into a program whereby farmers would be compensated for leaving land out of production and designating it for waterfowl habitat. I think that is a step in the right direction. However, one of the ways in which we can address the problem more fundamentally is to have the price of grain reflect the true cost of production. We would then not be forced to bring in these kinds of ad hoc programs such as paying farmers not to destroy natural habitat. The pressure would not be on them to farm this land in the first place.
The continuing low price of grain has driven western Canadian farmers to overuse, in my judgment, fertilizers and herbicides in an attempt to get a higher yield in the short term, again to compensate for lower prices. However, it is reaching the point of diminishing returns. More and more is being put into the same piece of land by way of these additives or environmental externalities. It is not just a question of a guaranteed return for farmers; it is a question of having an agricultural system which does not have all these unintended effects, both with respect to habitat and to soil conservation and quality.
So 1 repeat, we have an opportunity here to pass this motion and create a committee which will have the unique opportunity of looking at all these questions. 1 firmly believe that we cannot continue to put farmers in the position they have been in for so long. We have taken advantage of the fact that farming, unlike a great many other things people do for a living in Canada today, is a vocation. It is an intergenerational vocation. It is a heritage. It is something people do because that is the way they are. They farm because they are farmers. They farm both out of a sense of their vocation and out of a sense that they are doing something worth-while in producing the necessities of life, long after it has become not profitable to do so.
Farmers can only do that for so long. We cannot expect them to continue out of this sense of vocation for ever and ever. I am reminded of a joke I heard which illustrates this all too painfully. A fellow went into a store one day and bought a $10 hammer. He then went out and sold the hammer for $5. He then bought two more hammers for $10 each and again went out and sold them for $5 each. He kept buying more and more hammers for $10 and selling them for $5, until finally the storekeeper could not contain his curiosity any longer and asked the man why he was doing that. He asked how the man
August 17, 1987

could expect to make a living. The farmer said: "Well, it is not great but it's better than I was doing before when 1 was farming". This is the kind of situation in which farmers find themselves today. They constantly have to sell their produce at a price lower than the cost of production.
The other version of that joke is that the fellow selling the hammers replied: "If I could only sell enough of them, I might break even". That is again the situation in which farmers find themselves. I repeat the call which was issued so long ago by a true Tory, not one of these neo-Conservative Yankees who sit across from us today. John Diefenbaker was a true Tory from western Canada and he said: "Western Canadian farmers want parity not charity". Let the Conservatives show that for once they will act in line with that tradition and pass this Bill today when it comes to a vote.

It is certainly obvious, Madam Speaker. I am appropriately chastised. I sometimes lose my cool when I talk about agriculture, since it is such a hot topic.
As I was saying, there is a crisis in western Canada. You are not from western Canada, Madam Speaker, but as you know, there is a crisis there. There exists a double-whammy in western Canada in that the economy depends on the oil industry and on agriculture. Those are the bases of the economy of western Canada. I know that the Government has been trying to diversify the economy. It came up with a western diversification scheme. We in the New Democratic
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
Party announced our ideas on trying to diversify the western Canadian economy. There have been lots of ideas with respect to such areas as tourism, new industries, manufacturing, trade, Asian-Pacific matters, as well as specializing in technological goods and so on. But in spite of all these efforts the western Canadian economy for the foreseeable future will still be based on the twin pillars of oil and agriculture. In British Columbia, which is my area of the country, the economic base is forestry.
The Bill before us standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) proposes to tackle one of those areas, namely, the farming area. I note that when he spoke on this Bill on March 2, 1987, as reported at page 3737 of Hansard he said:
In essence, this particular Bill proposes the establishment of a floor price for agricultural products that has some reflection in the cost of production and a decent return for farmers. This Bill is proposing that, like workers who have a trade union or businessmen and professionals and their associations, farmers should have some guarantee that the price they receive will support them and their families in the production of food.
What this Bill tries to do is to give farmers some guarantee with respect to the prices that they will receive.
The Bill deals with wheat-and I will come back to that in a minute since we do have a form of parity pricing for wheat-as well as oats and barley which are now marketed through the Canadian Wheat Board. It also deals with pork and beef since there are no marketing boards for those particular products. The Bill would establish a price that would reflect parity for what a farmer receives for grain with the costs of production and a decent return for his product. This applies only to domestic consumption. We cannot do this on the international level because we are a signatory to GATT. I am informed that there is a $7 domestic price for wheat while the international price can be $3 to $3.50 per bushel. So there can be differences in pricing. This has been done with wheat and there have been no technical difficulties, that is to say, price parity for agricultural products that are domestically consumed. We are talking here about 9 per cent or 10 per cent of the grain that is produced by our farmers.
1 now wish to draw a parallel to oil since 1 am the energy critic for my Party. There was a proposal put forward by small oil producers in western Canada when they bought and went out of the oil market. The small oil producers said: "Look, for a level of production give us a floor price". When the price went to, say, $10 a barrel they said: "Give us a floor price of $15 per barrel for a limited period and we will pay that back. That will keep us going, keep us living and we will pay it back later". They said, quite properly: "When the price of oil goes up through the roof the Government puts on a ceiling price," as was done in the early 1980s under the auspices of the National Energy Program. Some of these proposals have already been tried in terms of a ceiling price. They could be implemented as well in terms of a floor price. This could also be done in the area of agriculture.

August 17, 1987
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
What does the Bill before us deal with? I have indicated that it deals with areas other than wheat. Why is the Bill drafted in the way that it is? It is difficult for a private Member to produce a Bill that calls for a subsidy or a deficiency payment. That is why the Hon. Member has drafted his Bill in the way in which he has. I point that out to Members of the House so that they will understand and perhaps support the Bill.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) in the remarks which he just completed said that we could create a committee that would have a unique opportunity to look at these questions. On the basis that these are emergency questions and on the fact that the farmer is really hurting and that here is a proposal that could and would work, it would be worth the time of the House to pass this Bill and to get a committee to look at the matter.
1 would also like to express a couple of other opinions that are related to the matter. People say that we have a great surplus of food. Indeed, in the developed countries, especially in the European common market and the European Economic Community, as well as here in Canada, we have a surplus of food. But we do not have a surplus of food when we look at the whole world. There are still people dying of starvation in this world. Surely, in 1987, on the international level we are capable of eliminating starvation, either through taking some of our surpluses from the rich world and giving them to the developing world, or by developing agricultural efficiency in the Third World, which is an even better solution. Some countries have been doing this, in particular India. That country just celebrated its fortieth anniversary of independence. There was a great deal of comment at the time about the difficulties that India has. But one of the good things that India has managed to pull off is its increased agricultural selfsufficiency.
Is it possible to do this? Is this Bill a possibility? 1 draw the attention of Members of the House to the remarks of our farm critic, the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), who spoke in the House on April 7 of this year. As reported at page 4955 of Hansard he said:
In spite of all the rhetoric I heard this afternoon from some of the Conservatives who spoke on this motion, this country is doing some of that right now. We have a two-price system for wheat at the moment, based at $7 a bushel for wheat consumed in this country, which comes close to the cost of production. We are doing that, and it is not wrecking the economy particularly, neither is it doing a whole lot of good.
However, it applies only to domestically consumed wheat used for human consumption and does not go quite as far as the Bill which was presented by my friend, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville, which would include wheat, oats and barley consumed by livestock and used for other purposes of animal and poultry production.
I think the Hon. Member makes the point that this has been done to a limited extent with wheat. That was not the entire solution since there are still some problems that exist. However, it was a step forward.
1 want to say that 1 had the experience a couple of months ago to be out in Calgary. I went north of Calgary to visit a vet and his family. The family I visited is named Sutmoller. Mr. and Mrs. Sutmoller took me to their house for the afternoon. They took me out into the neighbouring fields around Car-stairs, Alberta, and explained some of the problems.
I recognize the fundamental problems of the Canadian farmer. I submit to the House that the Bill presented by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville goes some way to helping solve some of those problems.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity to participate in the debate and take advantage of the few remaining moments to talk about parity pricing and some of the deficiencies in that particular proposal, at least as I understand them.
First of all, 1 wish to state that we are very much in agreement with our friends in the New Democratic Party and in the Official Opposition when we say that we believe Canadian farmers are deserving of assistance from Governments at both levels. That is the reason that during the course of the last 12 months the federal Government has provided an unprecedented amount of financial assistance to Canadian farmers, particularly to western Canadian farmers.
The largest difficulties being experienced are in the grains and oil seeds sector, which is the primary part of the agricultural economy. I wish that some of the provincial Governments, particularly of western Canada and my own Province of Manitoba, were more supportive. If the two levels of Government could co-operate, and there has never been a time in Canadian history when there was a greater need for cooperation, then the financial position of Manitoba farmers would be improved, if we could match the programs offered by the Alberta and Saskatchewan Governments.
The idea of parity pricing certainly has a surface appeal, which is perhaps one of the reasons why it is misrepresented by many. It has not been misrepresented by those who have spoken today, but misrepresented by many as being a panacea to agricultural problems.
Unfortunately, the bulk of the farm dollars earned in western Canada are earned through exports. Throughout Canada as a whole, 50 per cent of agriculture income is received from exports. The figure of export income is greater in western Canada than it is elsewhere. To this point in time, one of the principal weaknesses of parity pricing is that it can do nothing to assist the price that agricultural exports earn in the world market. For example, with reference to grains and oil seeds, where the vast bulk of our product is sold in the international market, parity pricing would indeed not constitute any significant increase in agricultural income.
Appropriately, reference has already been made to the two-price system which we have for wheat production. We in western Canada are painfully aware that the two-price wheat system means very little, because it represents a very small part of our total sales.
August 17, 1987

1 would remind Members of the House that when the committee travelled across Canada 12 months ago it looked at two-price wheat. Many of the witnesses who appeared before the committee also talked about parity pricing. There was a consideration of the concept, although not in the way that the mover of this motion would prefer.
Unfortunately, when examined under the microscope of that committee, neither two-price wheat or parity pricing represented the significant solution to western agricultural problems that many had hoped. The reason is that there is no proposal in parity pricing to augment income for that 90 per cent of the wheat that is not consumed in the domestic market.
We need to focus our attention on how to do two or three things. In this highly competitive agricultural market in which we live, we should be focusing our attention on how to increase exports. In western Canada, we are pleased with the record of the Canadian Wheat Board in this regard. Most Members of the House know that the exports have reached a record level this year, despite the very intense competition which exists in the international market-place. The Wheat Board, and others, are to be complimented. We must continue to move in that direction.
It would appear from weather conditions in the west, both during the summer and during the last few days, that production this year will not be what it was last year. Therefore, there will not be the same surplus to dispose of as before. We are still carrying a surplus from the previous year's crop, so we must focus on market development.
It is exceedingly important that we continue to work in the international community to end the trade war which is destroying international markets. Canadian farmers are among the most productive in the world. I know that talking about a "level playing field" is similar to a hackneyed statement these days. But as they have demonstrated in the past, Canadian farmers can do exceedingly well when they are given an opportunity to compete with others in the world market without any foreign impediment.
The principal thrust of Parliament and the Government should be toward trying to resolve that trade war. In that regard, a number of people have distinguished themselves in providing leadership. Beginning with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), seconded by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), and others have provided unprecedented leadership in the international community in attempting to resolve the trade war which has destroyed the economy of so many wheat and grain producing countries.
In Canada we cannot afford to match the subsidies of the Europeans and the Americans. In fact, I would go further and say that both the Europeans and the Americans are now discovering that they too cannot afford to maintain the present
Parity Prices for Farm Products Act
policies. In the international community, there has been definite progress. There is evidence that the insane trade war is starting to wind down. There will not be any results for two or three years, I would think, and that is being somewhat optimistic. We must do what we can to resolve that particular trade war. We must pursue the policies that we have been pursuing. We must persuade the Americans and the Europeans that they are not helping their own producers. They are not gaining any additional share of the world market as they anticipated. In fact, we have gained it because of the quality of our product. We must persuade them as perhaps to persuade their own public I think they know that the only winners in this process are consumers in certain countries.
While that struggle goes on at the international level, with the co-operation of all Parties, and I must stress with the cooperation of the provincial Governments, we must continue to build upon the national and regional tripartite programs which are in existence.
The Western Grain Stabilization Program has generated unprecedented cash flows during the last 24 months. Unfortunately, that program is now virtually bankrupt, and it is being funded by the federal Government. Further amendments to that program will be necessary. We must do more in the area of red meat tripartite stabilization. There was a positive meeting recently in Quebec City. We must encourage more of the provinces to join.
What is necessary now is not the projection of certain formulas, which at first glance seem to be a solution to problems. What is needed now is co-operation among all levels of government and continued involvement of the farm organizations themselves. Never before have they had the say they have had in the last 18 months. They must continue to be an integral part.
With the two levels of Government working together, the cooperation of all of the provinces, the continued support of the farm community, an emphasis on resolving the problems at the international level, and in the meantime with continued amounts of massive federal and provincial cash injection into the economy, I think that we can get through the next two or three years until farmers have a chance to get back on an equal playing field. When they do, farm economies will rise to a level at which they deserve to be. Our farmers will quite easily and readily be able to compete, because they know that they are superior farmers, the quality of their product is superior, and their technology is superior. Therefore, we have a responsibility and I believe a commitment to provide that type of cash support until agriculture is back on its feet where it deserves to be.
